Surplus . £1,019,385 INDUSTRI*L BRANCEL—The number of Policies to exist- ence at 31st December last was 9,617,484, and the amount assured £93 390,879. The weekly premiums receivable in re.pect of these Policies amounted to £74,993 per week, or £3,899,646 per annum. The above number includes 246,152 free or paid-up Policies granted in lieu of discontinued assurances on which no pre- miums are payable. The average duration of all the Policies now in existence is about six and three-quarter years, and when the large amount of new business introduced in rrcent years is con- sidered, this is strong evidence of the success of the means which have been adopted to promote the stability of the business The results of the Valuation areas follows : Life Assurance Fund on 31st D cember, 1891 ... £8,582,207 Net Liability for Life Assorts, ce Policies including reserve for immediate payment of claims... ... 7,776.712

Surplus £805,495 Of this net liability upwards of £BOO,OOO is in respect of free Policies granted in lieu of discontinued assurances, and to provide for the increased benefits conferred on Industrial Policy-holders during the Quinquennium. It is worthy of remark that in the two Branches together there are 233,358 Policies assuring amounts of from £5O to £lOO each, producing an Annual Premium Income of up- wards of One Million Potindt, and of thee 54,777 are with weekly Premiums. 44,645 quarterly, 21,010 half-yearly, and 112,926 with annual premiums. When it is considered that every proposer for an amount of £5O and upwards has the option presented to him of paving the premiums in any of these methods, it is remarkable how many deliberately choose the weekly premiums, thus affording a strong illus- tration of the adaptability of Industrial Assurance to the wants of the public. With a view to secure accuracy, two Independent Valua- tions are made in both Branches. The valuation of nearly Ten Million Policies, divided into a very large number of groups and classes, has employed the energies of a staff of about 700 for many months. The arithmetical processes alone have involved an immense amount of labour and would have been almost impossible of accomplishment with- out the aid of the Arithorneter. no less then fifty of these In- struments having been employed. Tea al Id Sir Andrew Clarke, For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashieoed China which I keep. end the advice has been appreciated.
It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion.

Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, Anil one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all 04 is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into apiece, the lady of the housa will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let, me give you a eup a tea.' I say ' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup end fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of all Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powertul in its effects upon the nerv.mis system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produce. a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. It you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresk, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measnre--the old fashioned teaseooaful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within Asa minutes you must pour It off again, or it: will become wicked instead of good."
Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise, A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who hime for gotten what this old fashioned ea is like.

The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be toned tobe much wiler than that now in use, and the taste m 4, not be acceptable at trot owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to he much more suitable for the system, mil if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinr.ry use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. Oh, it's the way with pa's; the cost is always too salt for them." "SHE isn't all that fancy painted her !" exclaimed a rejected lover, "and worse than thato e isn't all that she paints herself." course. A HISTORICAL CONUNDRUM. What was the key with which the spirit of retribution unlocked the door of time to let in the French revolution Ananhy. AN old gentleman, on his return from a fashion- able tour, being asked who carried off the palm at watering-place " hops," laconically answered, " Frogs." AN old gentleman, having -lie-eiriivited by as acquaintance to go out antj see his country seatjt t, and forth 'it to be a stump in a largo (10W. rWIFE-"l, I Wish"you qpld invite young ~f essor , some day. IJosthq is dreadfully .ient-minded ; perhaps 00%411 tak ,our Cecilia." A BOY who can't 'stand on the back ~of a chair to hunt for supr on the top shelf of the pantry, must not expe:olf many of the good, thirige Aff this world. "He knows on which side his bread is battered," is now 'rendered, "He is aware of what portion of the stkilf of life the oleaginous product of the dairy is dispersed." "MUSIC,' said Dr.' Johnson, "is the least dill. agreeable of all noises." The learned Doctor did not know everything. He never lived next door to a cornet amateur or a piano-banging young

lady. WarEN you see two cats on a wood-shed looking one another malignantly in the eye and waving their tails in the breeze, it is'a sign of .a coming squall close at hand.—Young Probs. "How came that coat sleeve with such a big hole in it ?" indignantly asked a mother of her ten-year. old boy. " Well, ma," he replied, "the fact is, I laughed in my sleeve till I bu'sted it." " You see," said Colonel Fliqem, "I didn't marry the girl because she turned out a deceiver." "Yes," said a bystander, "and the deceiver she turned out' was Colonel Fliqem." LITTLE Andy having got to thehead of his class, his father remarks: "I hop* roull 'stay there now," to which; the thoughtful boy responds "Oh, no, pa, 'I don't think I ; I might get too proud." " Malawi," he asked, in that style which a big brother assumes when patronizing a little sister— "Marion, do you know that the earth turns round ?" "Of toe I does," answered• Marion, resenting the imputation of ignorance; "that's the reason I titmbles out of bed." A DIAN was telling of a fight he saw in the street, when a big fellow, picked up a stick to knock another's brains out, whereupon he rushed in between them to save the intended victim. At this point a little shaver, who had been listening intently, proudly exclaimed : "He couldn't knock any brains out of you, could he, father?" A noorort of divinity was once giving his class some instructions about preaching in such a way as to gain attention and approbation: " Young gentle- men," said he, "it's all contained in a nutshell. When you go to preach n the city, take your hest coat; when you go to preach in the country, take your best sermon." A POMPOUS young lawyer, in addressing an old judge, said: "If your honour please, it is written in the book of nature that the eternal law of—" "At what page 2" exclaimed the judgi: interrupting him—" at what page?" The pompous young lawyer was visibly embarrassed. SHE was cosily intrenched upon his shoulder, and they were very, very happy. "George," she whispered, and he bent his head to listen, "do you know what I would do if your love for me should cool?" "Would you die, deer?" he asked pas- sionately. "No, George; I would bring a suit for breach of promise." "COME here, my little Eddy," said a gentleman to a youngster of seven years of age, while sitting in a room where a large company were assembled, . "do you know me ?" "Yes, sir, I think I do." "Who am I, then? Let me hear." "You are the man who kissed Angeline last night in the drawing- room." MRS. HOMESPUN, to the village doctor—" And how is your patient getting on ?" Doctor—" He's getting convalescent, but--" Mrs. Homespun, interrupting him—" Gracious ! he isn't so bad as that, is he ?" Doctor, completing his sentence— But he isn't getting convalescent very fast." Mrs. Homespun, with a sigh of relief—" Well, there's some comfort in that, anyhow." "A MAN in lowa," says an exchange, "wanting to get; rid of a curious neighbour, called his attention to an old Revolutionary musket that hadn't been loaded for forty years. The curious neighbour borrowing the old musket, took it home, and under his manipulation the forty-year-old charge proved itself to be as good as new, and that neighbour is now legitsmattly indulging his curiosity in a land which is far better than lowa." AN old Scotch lady, who had no relish for modern church music, was expressing her dislike of the singing of an anthem in her own church one day, when is neighbour said: "Why, that is a very old anthem. David sang that anthem to Saul." To this the old lady replied : "Wed, wed, I noo for the first time understan' why Saul threw hi:. javelin at David when the lad sang for him." HE was the local doctor and everyone wondered why the parson appointed him churchwarden, especially those who aspired to the dignity them- selves. Oue of these, however, soon solved the mystery, and to his rival's discomfiture. "I know why the parson's 'pointed of him," be said, decisively. " Parson gets a fee for every funeral, and the doctor's guaranteed him a certain number every year, he has." , "I SAY, sir, do you want to hire a boy, sir ?" said a Inlght-looking little fellow, as he stepped into a butines ollice, " What can you do, sir?' was the respondent inquiry. "I can tell the truth, sir," was the bright reply. "Don't want you, my little man; my business can't stand truth-telling., "Better take the bey," said a bystander. " I know him. When he says he can tell the truth he lies. He can't do it, nor his father before him couldn't either." Boy engaged on modern business principles. ROWLAND BILL once became surety for a mem- ber of his church. The man failed, and the incautious pastor had to pay El 000—the amount of the bond. The same day on w Lich he discharged his liability, he called upon a friend, who, observ. Lug that he was unusally depressed, remarked, "Why, Mr, Hill, What's the matter with you to: ? You seem altogether heavy and uncomfort- able." "Heavy, sir," replied Mr. Hill; "you are quite mistaken there, for I am a thousand pounds lighter than I wa's yesterday." THE dearest spot on 'earth to me 1" as the young man murmured when his sweetheart coaxed him into an ice-cream saloon. "WOMEN," quoth Jona, "aye the salad of life, At once a boon and a blessiug." fif In one way they're salad, indeed," replied Brown, "they take so much time in their dressing."

Mr. Rettert Peel„whose successes at Montuearlo have created so much sensation, is the only.iim of Sir Robert Peel, and follows in the political foot- steps of his father. Curiously enough, Mr. Peel, when it Oxford, was the fellow-lodger and habitual comrade of Mil Coningsby Disraeli, in spite of the traditional hostility that separatted the bearers of these famous names imancient days. Mr. Peel has engaged himself to Miss Lane-Fox; who is a grand- daughter of Mr. Lane-Fox, of Bramham Moor, one of the few survivals of the old type, of. country gentlenien who adhere even in London to the small breeches of a bygone"generation.

The Provost and Fellows of King's College, Cam- bridge, did a kindly and gracious act when they spontaneously offered the use of their historic chapel fat a funeral service in memory of the late. Miss Clough, Principal of Newnham College. The sug- gestion was gratefully accepted, and hence it hap- pened that on Saturday afternoon a service in many respects unique was held in the magnificent chapel of King's. Never before at any funeral has been I such a concourse of black-robed women graduates. \From all parts of the kingdom had flocked score*of old Newnbara students, bent on paying a last lbv- ing tribup to one whom they owed so much.

In reference to the miniage lately annifiunced as about to take place between Mr. Norman Neruda, son of Lady Halle and Miss Mary Peyton, it may be interesting to remark that the young lady has sqme claim to athletic distinction. She is one ,of the best lady Alpine climbers in the *orld, atidL her pluck and endurance have excited the enthusiasm of both natives and tourists in Switzerland. She has as- cended the Matterhorn on the difficult Italian side, and got down the Zermatt, and has performed other bold Alpine feats with .4er finance, for they both believe in the Burns principle, " climb the hill together." Miss Peyton has recently been elected to the AuArian Alpine Club, and 18 proud of the honour. Mr. Neruda is a sound Liberal in politics and a member of the Eighty Club.

Since Brunel died the Great Western Company have not been conspicuous in the front ranks of railway progress; but the new departure which they have taken deserves special acknowledgment. While other c3rapanies are lavishing money in im- proving the accommodation of the unprofitable first-class passenger, the Great Western have started a saloon or " corridor " train, more or less on the American principle, to the benefits of which third-class passengers are admitted, and in which they will obtain some of the most substantial con- veniences supplied in the Pullman cars. This is a pleasant contrast to the policy of the South-Eastern Company, who have jute. been at great pains and 1 expense to build an American car train, reserved exclusively forthese who consent to pay the out- rageous first-class fares in force on that line.

Is it true, as alleged by a correspondent of the "Daily News," that the allowances made for" out- fit " to ambassadors and ministers on their removal from one post to another very far 'exceed the actual expenditure necessitated or actually incurred in consequence of these changes? If this be the case —and the correspondent writes as though he knew what he was talking about—the granting of these allowances is • simply a misappropriation of the public money. What earthly reason can there be why Lord Dufferin should receive £2,000 on his transfer from Rome to Paris, Lord Vivian £2,500 on exchanging Brussels for Rome, Sir H. D. Wolff £2,000 on removing from Teheran to Bucharest, and .12,000 more on going from Bucharest to Madrid, if they do not actually spend the money? It is noth- ing less than a robbery of the taxpayer that these highly-salaried diplomatists should get huge bonuses of this kind as an accompaniment to every stage in their promotion. . Z 134 Tile sentence on Mrs. Osborne is neither unex- pected nor unreasonable. It was generally thought she would get six months, and some people went as high as twelve months. There is no doult that but for the pathetic appeal of Mrs. Hargreave the sentence would have been ranch heavier, for Mr. Justice Smith is not the man to flinch from duty. This is the second most painful case he has bad to deal with. The other was the case of Captain Verney who was an old friend, and I believe an old school- fellow, of his lordship. The most sincere commisera- tion is felt for Captain Osborne and for the poor baby that will be born in prison about the month of June It was hinted in court, as I said a long time since that the original intention was that Mrs. Osborne should not surrender till after the birth of the child. Although it was not said so, this was ob- viously with the intention of sparing Captain Osborne's child the taint of prison birth. Captain, Osborne's devotion to his unhappy wife in her pun- ishment. which has been the theme of general admiration, was quickened by a generous recogni- tion of the fact that, trusting her innocence, be bad pressed her to go into court in the action against the Hargreaves, and had thus, as it were tempted her to perjury.

_ THE TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT had its real beginnings, and until now, has, with 'varying changes, held on its way. The ministers of all denominations gradually became total abstainers, and, have remained so. I think it would be difficult to find around Worcester half-a-dozen ministers who are not total abstainers, Temperance here finds supporters from two rather con- flicting, and difficult to reconcile, camps; those who rely on force, 'and those who stand on moral ground. The former of these can have, in my opinion, no permanent success ; the latter will surely be successful, appealing as they do to man's intelligence. The Puritans of old have left their mark, a mark that will never be eradicated, nor would I wish it to. After a sojourn of four years in San Pranciseo, I feel my self well able to make comparisons. These may be odious to the 'Frisco people, but none the less true. I am no Sabbatarian. Owing to the want of one or other of the cranial bumps, I am unable to lift what we call the seventh day, out of the ordinary course of things; but I shall certainly alway.B be on time when the question of keeping one day out of the seven out of the clutches of the capitalists is to the front. The contrasts between the city of WORCESTER AND SAN FRANCISCO ' are apparent. Turn out of a Sunday morning,say, in the latter city; drags of all kinds, and, almost for all purposes, are rattling' about the streets. The stores are open just as their owners'wish We do not walk far before we come adross one or other of the many nationalities, vindicating their rights of citizenship by carrying their. own particular country's flag, and thumping ont their national music. Book-stalls are out on the side-walks, and fruit vendors are roaring themselves hoarse in the gutters. If the Government has happened to fall foul of a " Kreutzer &mats" and prohibited it going through the mail, it is offered for the &filiation of those who happen to be church-inclined. There is no rest in all this. I have nothing to say against, but everything in favour of, a game of base-ball, or cricket for young men, but I do protest strongly against the feverish unrest, the constant whirl of the brain which is ever apparent in the State which boasts it has no Sunday Laws. Everywhere are to be seen brewers' drags carrying Dut beer. In every part of the city's centre saloons are almost as thick as the summer flies. On the main street, as on thu back streets,through the saloon doors and windows, are to be seen large paintings of nude women. As evening draws in music streamsup from "the dive;" a glance down the steps falls on the short skirts end fancy-coloured hose of some poor lass striving to earn "an honest penny." From noon until midnight the cars are crowded with patrons of the theatre. What these patrons go to see may be questioned from the lithographs that decorate the walls. It would re- quire a much more lively pen than mine to sketch this city of the Pacific slope., One feature only re- mains with me. A continental Sunday with all the freedom it can possibly surround itself with, does not necessarily mean a free and happy Sunday for the working-man. I know there are write ts whd make vigorous efforts to paint the city in more at- tractive colours. I state what I have seen, yet not ' all, and I have no interest in selling corner lots, or booming real estate. (To be concluded next week.) •
"THE OLD BLOODY STONE."

(A LANCASHIRE LEGEND.) At Newton-le-Willows, a long time ago, A terrible battle was fought, When the Puritan forces defeated the.foe, And a cavalier earl was caught. The battle rag'd fiercely o'er valley and"dale,— IsTo quarter was given or asked; And very few lived to tell the sad tale, For pity was brutally masked. One gallant old Colonel, as good and as brave
As ever-uplifted a sword, Was bent to an ignominious grave,
_ . By the savage and desperate horde. And they captur'd his loving, courageous wife, As 13 h eyisorrowing, searched o'er the slain. For him who was dearer to her than life, r

Vinous she never would see again. And there, in a nook of the " Gallows Croft," They cruelly put her to death ; While a prayer for her murderers went aloft, That she breathed with her dying breath. They buried her poor headless trunk below An enormous red bouhler stone ; From thence—as the terrified travellers know— There issues full many a groan. 'Tis said, that at " Midnight's witching hour," When the village is " bathed in sleep," The stone is upraised with a .myStical power, And the lady is heard to weep. And her suffering spirit seems ever to say, " Oh. woe far the murderers grim, Who, without one small touch of humanity's ray, Killed this frail, helpless body, and Him "Oh, why are the Miniones of Blood allowed To slay at a King's curst command; And envelope their kin in a gory shroud,— The Pride and the Flower of the Land? "Oh. woe for the monarchs who cry 'Peace, peace, And are secretly urging on war; Whose black preparations seem never to cease— These, these do my spirit abhor! "Oh, why does the Ruler and Monarch of all— Who knows all our minutest needs, And cares for the meanest of objects that fall— Permit such sanguineous deeds? "Oh, why must my rest"—but the sorrowful moan Is stilled, for a scare passer-by, Has rubbed with his foot after moist'ning the stone With his spittle, to stifle the cry. . There be those who believe in the wild legend still, Who, if forced to go nigh there at night— Despite of a strong and courageous will— Would be paralyzed almost with fright. And the little ones tremble and shudder with fear, And dread to be left all alone, When in solemn, mysterious accents, they hear The "'Lay of the Old Bloody Stone." TUM OPEN. Newton-le-Willows, 10, 3, `92.

F VG+ CHAPTER XX. - --- - ' . Kr, OL YIP MALE 'ltiffirfT9i(a yartirvi ttne.mever knows where Jack is, si.nce epe• came a Asquire of !dames !" repeated Madam, ,anesur. ingly. Lady Callerley leant against the gate, and i returned. her significant look with a calm„ sad, questibi4g„gaze. She Walte 4 i6r -Mrs. Breamish to carrysimithe attack hair Igiffering. . ' t WW,eVer is, the attpac*Vi:pi,this place of the tombs, Silvia, that one of your gay temperament shoulfl choose it-for the )3c9e of yeur,orditations / Do you kilo* the reputhtidn it has Of being hap.uted;l Can you lipt fancy all the spectres that must' heVer round Web' 13iickly populated grave-'. But perhaps you are 'not supe'rstitioills`?=. AltbiAikli I' fancied I lad' heard 'something to the eatfb.ry from old Nanny Widdringtrin •!' or perhaps' ..?' If it were a love tryst 'now, olio could Uniterstand such a morbid taste. 'There would be _ . . .

7-7 Othething to say then in its favour, and its lone. lirteisa and bad name would be. all the, greater inducement for frequenting it!" silvia still looked calmly rat her enemy,. for enemy she felt 'sure Doisethy Breamish was. ' "Do you think it is a love tryst ?" she asked, in, , Att.tat• tone. • 3.lida.M. gave one') of her uncanny laughs, thoSe ,laugha o,void of mirth. , "Dear me,,ehild, how sharply you take one up I Is it at all likely that I should have mentioned it if II had believed such to be the case? Nor would I' i willingly play gooseberry. to you, little one ! But see I My old horse is hungry, and thinks the grass here very inviting. He is too spiritless to run away, so if you will take hold of his head I ,*ill diknount, and join you in your meditations for
a few minutes.

, Mrs. Breandsh; who was very light and active for lso fine a woman, was by •Lady Callerley's side im- ,mediately. Then, throwing up the reins, she allowed her steed, to, follow his own sweet will; knowing that he was pretty safe hot to leave the lush grawrgrowing near at hand for the more scanty !pasturage of the And banks. , , , Gathering up her habit, she 'noised through the , who was feeling tired arid not very strong,. went back to her seat on the flat tomb- stOne. ' • Madani followed her etataple. "You are quite certain I shall not be in the way?" she queried, in a soft, insinuating voice. -Silvia did not deign to answer what she felt to be an inuendo. .
Although she was acutely conscious of acting injudiciously in not trying to throw Madam 'off, guard, it was not possible for her to act other-
wise. This woman, Dorothy Breamish, hated her with a living hatred that was growing stronger every day. And of a certainty there was no love lost be- tween them. ' • •
Lady Callerley, therefore, being young and im- pulsive, and inexperienced in the diplomacy quired by the situation, would have preferred the honest course; and would fain have ceased any

, pretence pf friendship. _ But alas, conventionality demands lies, and insists upon hypocrisy, especially upon the part of women. . - Madam's sharp claws were veiled judiciously be- neath velvet, and thought Silvia's instinct warned her of them, she found it difficult to resent their existence; and equally difficult to smile and look pleasant when they peeped out for a moment. An instance of the native deceit of the woman was

iown in the fact that while she was compliment- ing Lady Callerley upon her improved 'looks, and saying how well the air of the North seemed to agree with her, since it gave pi her complexion p tint like unto, the petals of a wild rose, who would ' have guessed that she was watching that same lovely colour come and go fitfully, and saying to herself in triumph, " Consumptive evidently! hectic colour, and eyes too brilliant. If she lives through the next three months, a severe winter will try her constitution. Nervous too, and ex- citable. Old Nanny's stories have 'done her no good." Such cold-blooded calculation is almost incredible in any woman, but Madam was not as others of her sex. Sometimes it seemed as though the devil got possession of her entirely, and she became in his hands a mere puppet. She was growing to hate Lady Callerley for other reasons than because the latter had usurped the place she had once fondly imagined would be her own. • The love—if it an be dignified by such a title— which had been stifled within, her by her 'cousin's prolonged absence, jiad •• come to life again during these latter months of companionship ; and now glowed within her, a fierce consuming flame. .

While Mrs. Breamish was studying and noting Silvia's altered looks; Lady Callerley, on her side, was planning and contriving how best to introduce the subject lying nearest her heart. What was the best course to pursue to get the secret, if secret there was, out of Sir Lancelot'l cousin? Would Madam refuse to impart it because of hie probable displeasure? Or would she also wisl to hide it as something derogatory to the family - Silvia was not clever at beating about the bush, and after all her meditations broached the subject in a perfectly tactless manner. She turned and looked Madam straight in the face. `."Bell me a story, Mrs. Breamish?" she said abruptly, "you are very good at recounting ok legends." "Does that mean a compliment or the reverse I may take it either way, I suppose. It may he flattering to my dramatic capabilities—or it ma) mean that I am dull company otherwise ? " "I do not mean the latter. You are never dull,' replied Silvia simply. Madam laughed again. "What story is it you wish me to recount, little flatterer," asked Madam lightly. "I fancy yot have some particular one in your mind ? " Lady Callerley hesitated, and gave a restless sigh. "Yes, yes, there is one that I wish to hear !'- she said at last, " it is the story of this very place we are in—the story of this old ruined church. l know that there is one. Old Nanny Widdringtor admitted as much, though she would not tell it. She referred me to you, and said you were sure tc tell it to me if I enquired? It is connected with —with the Callerleys, I believe. Soinething about a hunt she said—a run to death which began here and ended—ah, she did not say where." Mrs. Breamish looked out of her eyes in a side- way sinister fashion. "Yes, I know the story," she said slowly, and with apparent reluctance, " but I may not tell it you. You are nervous, child ! " "No, no, I am not nervous—at least not by nature. It is only when I keep on dreading and dreading, and imagining all sorts of horrors, that I get afraid. But when I know what I have to face, be it ever so bad, I can be brave enough. Even Teddy says so, though he does laugh at me sometimes ! "You do not like to fight with shadows! But suppose it is just shadows that you have to dread, shadows of the past—their influence upon those nearest and dearest to you? What then? Will your boasted courage avail you, or will you then turn coward and wish your fate were not • inter- woven with that of a doomed family ? " Mrs. Breamish spoke in a slow, solemn tone, fraught with prophetic sadness. Silvia shivered, but she answered firmly enough, that even so she had rather know the worst at once. Madam gripped her arm and looked straight into her eyes. "So be it! Remember it is you that have sought to know—l have not sought to tell you! Promise me moreover that you will never let Lancelot find out who enlightened you on this point of family history—history or superstition— call it which you will." ' "I promise ! " "That will do. You know how averse he affects to be to old stories and legends! I seem always telling them to you, though, Silvia, spite of that same aversion of his. Perhaps, after all, I ought not to tell you this," she mused, with pro- voking slowness, and well assumed roluetance. ' "You will do it, nevertheless " replied Silvia, with considerable heat. "Well, well, child! Remember that 'when ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise.' But since you are bent upon folly, I must e'en give way. I suppose my story ought to begin in the regular style of once upon a time' ?" Begin how you like—only do begin 1"
CHAPTER XXI.
A RUN TO DEATH.
lic'te it ta 3=—_

n Callerleys have been for the most part a Ilawless race—no imputation upon your m master, Silvia, who was always an exem- ,ln in every relation of life—yet have they not-teen wanting at times in a certain strain of fanaticism. Those of them who have been reli- hard, )rting 1
ously disposed have taken their piety in a hard, ,Itgted-lßtoler&flt-kul4- of- way,. more- comforting to their own self-righteousness than pleasant to those who did not shire the same belief. Duirieg
ifitTime.=Oft-ke7Pfilitilii37 *hen Nlr- itbhcrAfrwasrile in the land, this strain of fanaticism broke out-in lgolonel Larieelot Calfoil6y7-'brolte.bfitivs:sl Reelect

:frenzy of hatred towards ihs'tv poor witches:" " Colonet-Lanclidot, CallerTey!" interrupted Silvia !hastily, "Is that the hateful-looking man Whose !portrait so greatly resemh.le@ my husband ?" „ " :040(4 tetice, carer said, IY.la4am,, latt9ol hig, and shaking' a playfnil, forefinger, at the girl. "You ought' not to .find ,any man who resembles your husband, 'hateful looking However lam .bound to ctiofess that Colonel Callerley ha not' a pleasing expression." , „. "Go on with your story,' please !" • "There is small doubt, judging from the number of wofnen found -ghilty bf witthc.taft hereabouts, that thieisheinoaS 'offence was exceedingly prevalent i,n this 'County of Northumberland, and that it needed all the zeal of godly,,men to root it out. Colonel •Lancelot- Callerley was 4. gc4dly, man, there-

- . fore he d§nleyed,doiagthis-duty in-I-this-respect, 1, "As other,parf fOilhd'their pleasiirein the chase, Colonel CallerleY delighted in nothing 'so much as the -hunting, ~cven -.lto/ loath, of these .nialignant witches; who wer'e,- iindObAndly, the 'plague' of limiest far merl/41tives,,bi beWitching their cows, so, Abet, they withheld their milk, and by laying spells upon churns 'tO' prevent theliitter froth coming,' and by doing other much More 4,rieked. and•cliead-, ful things. Doubtless suCh is these deserved their fats; but, as so • often happens, the innocent were frequently punished for the guilty. When awiteh- 'finder gets a profit out of every wretched woman wliom he does to death, it is reasonable to suppose , he win go on discovering tresh ones wno are im- pervious: to Tin-pricks, and who have somewhere upon their bodies the mark of the evil one. But, , of coin* Calleilers motive was a much higher one; and -le, had the satisfaction of thinking that I he was. doing. God's work. ' "One night he we riding alone past this old chili*. which wilthen, even as now, in a ruinous condition, when, to his astonishment, he perceived it to be brilliantly lighted up, as though for service. At once; with quick intuition, he suspected that unholy- rites were proceeding within the sacred precincts; and taking his horse to a gatepost, he crept up to one of the windows and looked in. His fears—or perhaps more truly his ' hopes—were verified. .A terrible, sight met his eyes. In the chancel burned 'a fire, over which a cauldron was 'suspended, and to and fro around it went groups of hags, casting in 'their loathsome contributions, one by one, to help the hell broth that was simmering there. ' AS they did so, they kept muttering in- -cantations all the While. The lamps which, flared and flickered on every side against the walls were formed out of human skulls. , "Nothing dismayed, but all aglow, instead with righteous indignation, Callerley leant his shoulder against and burst Open' the 'dolif, and drawing his sword, rushed into the midst of the devilish crew. Alas; , for his weak 'human power. In, a moment the 'lights were -extinguished, mocking laughter ' sounded all around hini',::in the darkness, and he was left alone in the ruined church, With the night Wind whistling though it. It was too bad. - Most folks would have thought he had got off only too easily from such a foolhardy enterprise. But in the cause of righteousness Colonel Callerley knew no • fear, and his rage and inclignatien were boundless' when the friends of Satan , flew ~.aff thus unscathed, and he was not even allowed the pleasure of attack: big them. 'Judge, then, of hie delight when, riding slowly homeward, he saw before him, on the road one of' these 'same witches; a •wretched, feeble, decrepit creature, who had evidently forgotten her broom- , 'stick, since.the means of ,flight , were denied her, and she Was left to be his prey. With a cry of rapturous, fury he chased, and ran her to death, just as he reached Yarrop Burn. , Without a moment's hesitation he pie ced the helpless creature through the body disregarding . all her lir piteous cries for mercy. s rage to kill had, ren- dered him both blind and deaf for the time being,

and it was not until he stood beside the dying form of the old woman that he recognised it for that of old Elspith Dunn, his nurse and foster- mother. She, however, knew him only too well. With her last breath she cursed him and all those of his sex who should come after him and bear his name. Whether one is superstitious or no, Silvia, one can scarcely fail to acknowledge that a strange fatality has ever pursued the masculine portion of the family. ' You must• have noted that fact, child, if you have paid any attention to the Callerley history at all.' • Silvia did not reply. Her face had grown very white arid rigid, and her eyes were fixed on the far off horizon with an intensity of horror growing into them. She was trying to pierce to mists of the future, and the dim, gigantio nightmare that loomed there appalled her young imagination. Was there no escape from this frightful doom! Truly, she was not strong enough to fight with shadows 1 "What words were those the witch said when she was dying ? " she asked, in an awe-stricken whisper. ' "It would be difficult to answer that question accurately,' Silvia !" replied Madam shrugging her shoulders; "tradition adds to, and detracts from, old Sayings, until little of the original form re- mains. It was. Something of this sort, 'He had drunk in her Milk as a child, and yet that had not held him back from being her murderer, so for his sake all the men of his race should die out of their beds'; and the water which ran past them, dyed with her blood, should prove fatal to the first and the last Lancelot Callerley.' Colonel Lancelot, as you remember, was drowned crossing the burn on horseback one night:before the bridge was built. There has never been a Lancelot since, until the late squire, who was, like your husband, opposed to superstition, insisted upon giving his heir the , old family namp. "'there, you have had the story, little one, and now you must let me depart. Why, how pale you are, dear Silvia I I wish now that I had not told you the superstition. But you would have it, you know, and you assured me that you were not nervous I" There was a cold and devilish malice in Mrs. Ereamish's glance, that roused Silvia to some sort of self command. At least the woman should not have leave to gloat over the tortures she was in- flicting. "jo no I I do not feel nervous, not nervous at all, 'Hrs. Breamish I Only it is so—so very amusing —your story, with its witches, and all that sort of rubbish, ha, ha! Just as though anyone would believe in dooms and fatalities nowadays. You don't, do you, Dorothy ? " Madam was not taken in by this show of scep- ticism. She mounted her horse, and then stooped to fire a parting shot in Silvia's ear. "Pray ,that your child may be a girl, Lady Callerley, ' she whispered, and rode off briskly through the grey twilight. • Silvia clung to the gate for as long as she was in sight • then sank down upon the long grass trembling in every limb, and moaning a little to herself, but softly, like a dumb creature in pain. A gentle, wailing, melancholy wind was creeping along the ground, bowing the broad white hemlock flowers and the rank vegetation that grew amongst the neglected graves. A sense of fear overpowered Silvia, and she scarce dared to lift her eyes lest they should light upon some of those restless ghosts whose bones lay so uneasily beneath the waters. The very grass seemed alive with weird spectral shapes as the winds crept over it, billowing it with silvery waves. And all these spectral shapes cri,ed to her, and they all cried one thing, with their mocking fiendish voices. • - _

" Doomed, doomed, doomed ! Your husband is doomed; and your child is doomed—if it be a boy. Doomed, doomed, doomed !" She tried to rise and flee from the haunted place; but just at that moment the wind, from wailing and melancholy, rose to a sudden fury, and came surging through the ruined walls, with yells of tempestuous agony. There was something un- earthly about tMs sudden gust. It proved the climax to the girl's terror; bore her down, over- whelmed her, as in a great sea of misery; and with a wild despairing cry, she succumbed to it, and lost consciousness

* * * * * * * Jack Breamish had been shooting rabbits in the twilight, and was coming back along the links with his gun under his arm, when his attention was attracted by something white which was' lying just within the wall of the old churchyard on the cliff. His eyes were pretty sharp, but he could not define this mysterious white object. It was too big to be a bird, even a great dead gull with out-stretched wings. He laid down.his gun,, and approached it cautiously. What was his astonishment to find it resclve itself into the uncele:vittur4l,oti‘of Lady Callerley, stretched milt:al the 44,10,—daa'y ; a,l her

ON THE 81:11P CANAL.

div.head: STOCKTON 'HEATH TO .ACTON GRANGE.
div.p: STOCKTON 'HEATH TO .ACTON GRANGE.
By Lookiii-Orr.

A fair space 'of time has elapsed since I was in close touch with the Canal in the neighbourhood I of Warrington, and perhaps a few "impressions" which were impressed by a stroll last Monday, between Stockton Heath and Acten Grange may just be worth a limited portion of your space, The canal up in that directiOn is not such a busy, place as it used to be, but in the neighbour- hood of Twenty-step Bridge, Stockton Heath, there are a few lively locomotives still puffing about as though business was brisk; and, looking off to the right, one sees that two or three steam navvies are hard at work shifting material which the navvies—l mean the flesh- and-blood navvievi this time—describe by a single, I expressive, but not very refined word, but which we will speak of as matter in the wrong place I —very much in the wrong place in fact for the Ship Canal shareholders. Time works changes especially in the way one regards steam navvies. A few yeariago—people who have shares in the Canal will.be able to specify the iexact time much better than I can—the steam navvy was a wonder and a curiosity in this locality, but that feeling has almost passed away and tip sharp snort and rattle. of the mechanical digger attracts little more atten— tion than the noise of the passing vehicle. What- was at one time a novelty has now become—well, not quite, but very nearly an antiquity. Under the Canal near Twenty-step bridge there is being, or rather has been, for I*believe it 'it now almost completed, constructed a capacious brick subway through which to carry past the canal the gas, water and sewage pipes of the locality. Turning away to the right along the new road that. has been made one.soon..gets intp , the neighbourhood of Lower Walton. And, by the way, these new roads which have been constructed at the expense of the Canal Co., will be not one' of the least benefitt3 conferred on this locality by the great undertaking. They will be a Convenience and a benefit to the general com- munity, but they will be of particular benefit to the land owners. Everything, in fact, seems to bring grist to the landlord's mill. They are paid well for the land that iStaken from them, and then they have a good lumplif what is left to them nicely opened out free of charge for building sites. This is seen by the fact that already new houses have been erected and tenanted by the tide of the new read from Stockton vleath to Walton. Of late the neigh- bourhood of Tom Paine's bridge has been one of the busy points on the canal. Near there the Chester road is now carried over the canal by a temporary bridge,and the soil underneath has been completely scooped avv,ay, so that what used to be a pretty sub- stantial barrier betvfnen one part of the canal and another has been removed,the " cutting " being now open from Stockton Heath to Acton Grange. Near Tom Paine'a bridge, too, a few workmen are giving the finishing touches to one of those rather expen- sive incidental works of which there are so many in connection with the canal: This is the laying of a chain of large iron pipes, of about four feet in diameter, which are to convey the waters of the Old Quay canal from the point where it is blocked up near Twenty-step bridge away in the direction of Acton Grange so as to keep up the watei supply at the works of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, near Runcorn.

But, passing along towards Lower Walton, one notices that the Stag Inn, which was at one time supposed to be doomed to extinction—so far as the present structure goes at all events—is still in exist- ence. A few yards further on a commencement has been made with the'new'road which' is to runfrom that Point through Arpley Fields 'to' 'Wild erspool CansevraY. Nothing beyond a startg6ems to have been thine here, but much progress has been Wade with the swing bridge which is to carry this road- way over the Canal, and on Monday h considerable number of men were busy preparing,• the founda- tions of the road at the point where it will cross the site of the Old Quay Canal. This readway, I may mention, will add another,lhough on a minor scale, to the many embankments which already diversify the landscape in the neighbourhood of Warrington. The embankment will commence almost directly' the roadway gets over the Canal and continue till it reaches the river, over which it will pass by means of it fixed MO level bridge, and it will thence de- scend by means of another embankment which will stretch across Arpley Meadows almost to the cricket kriiund. To ,write like this of long-drawn out embankments may perhaps seem .rather appal ling to the careful teain-ownet who is likely to make much use of; the road, but there is nothing to be afraid.of. The. gradients are ea y. On the south side of the river the roadway, will rise by a gradient of one in 172, which, to the untrained eye, will practically seem to be a level road. On the north side of the river the gradient will be rather steeper being one in 100, ,but,e,ven this will not be found to be anything to grumble.at. It. will be-noticed that the new road is to-pass over the yer.,by means of a permanent high level bridge. Under the former scheme the new roadway would !have crossed the river in a line with the dam; that is to be built there, but the new proposals of the" can ',COmpany pontain a provisisn that the dam shell nOw"be- constructed a short- distance nearer Wilderspool: The Mani will be pierced With a lock of the dimensions of 125 ft: by 25ft,, to allow of the passage of vessels from the new docks to the river, and ,vice-versa, From Lower Walton Village up to• Acton Grange, the canal seems to be altogether clear of workmen, and indeed, the niakhig.of tlie canal so far as this short length .is concerned, 'appears to be all but complete .f At Acton Grange the ,en*gies of the I worktnen live largely concentrated *On the great railway bridge,' which, looked 'at from a distance, seems to be a stupendous piece of work, but which .at close quarters, when one looks at .4the, massive masonry, and immense quantity of intricate network of-timber uSAd 'as' supports, is even mare ,imposing' and stupendous. Tbe Chairman read a letter he had received frern Col: McCorquodale in.reply to one he had addressed to him at the Beard's request,wishing him to re-consider the matter of his resignation.—Colonel McCorquodale said,referring to the chairman's letter and their interview, to far as his (the Colonel's) feelings were concerned he would much -prefer remaining a member of the Board to deserting his old friends. Be had considered it was net Correct 'on nis part to continue a'member of the Board while he was unable to attend with some degree of' regnlafity. However, the Commissioners had treated his propoetion with such generosity, that he felt bound to comply with their request, and should hope to be at their March meet lug and as many subsequent ones as possible, it being tleariy understood'lthat he would vacate his seat whenever • the .yeepayers desired to send a delegate to look after their interests in his Place. He concluded with many thanks to the Commissioners for the consideration shown to Min.—The Chairman said he presumed the Board were .j all very Willing to accept the withdrawal of Colonel MeCorquodale's resignation. He (the chair- man) was very glad " himself that the Colonel retained his seat. At he said he hoped to attend the meeting a little more regularly than he had done, hp (the chair- man). had no doubt that he would as in the past be of service to the ratepayers and the Commissioners., Be moved that they, accept the withdrawal of the resigns- Mdekation seconded, and the motion was TIIK WATRR SUPPLY or CROW-TANI. ' , The Chairmanieed a letter from' Mr. J. W. Thorpe, drawing attention to complaints made about scarcity of water in Cre y-lane. The Chairman explained that there had been a difficulty through an air vessel bursting, on .Sunday, and after this hid, been repaired and the 'w'ater turned: on to the main, the wrong valve was turned bid the water was stopped from ,going into the tank. and caused. one Of the main pipes to burst. Tat was remedied as soon as possible, and the water got in again on Monday afternoon. Since then there had been a plentiful supply .of water so far as he knew. But he wat,given to understand that unless their tank ,was kept lull of water, some parts of the district the supply did not reach. Mr. Brierley had written to him about it and he had replied that he must always keepthe tank full.. He did not think from what Mr. Brierley had said over and over again, that the tank was sufficiently high to supply the higher parts of the town, therefore it was for the Commissioners to consider what was to be done.

This Committee's minutes contained the following : Ordered on the Motion of the Chairman that the special Gas Committee's proceedings of November 28, 1891, as ,revised, be approved and adopted, and that Mr. Brierley prepare an estimate of the cost of the proposed exten- sion for the next meeting. The special Gas Committee having considered the necessity of lighting Newton Commons lock and adjoining road, made recommenda- tions for providing this. The report was adopted. Mr. Ockleston addressed a number of his supporters. He Said he was sorry that they had not won but they had made a good fight and having-reduced the majority to 41, had no cause to be disheartened. (Applause.) He hoped they would win on a future occasion.—Mr. J. Faulkner said e,onsidering the forces they had had to battle against, they had one very well indeed, but he hoped next time they would have all their workers shoulder to shoulder and be enabled to turn.,that small minority into a majority of several hundreds. lApplause.) —Mr. W. Handley said seeing that it was Mr. Ockle- ston's first essay in public life, it was not an unsatis- factory achievement to have reduced the majority to 41, and he was certain that victory would have been theirs had those who had been accustomed to work with them, worked with them on that occasion. It would be gener- ally admitted that they had suffered defeat at the hands of their own friends. (Applause.) But he should not like hard words said, because he believed they were sincere in their belief that local elections should not be political, and he believed at the coming Parliamentary elections they would find them shoulder to shoulder along with them. (Applause.) He thought that the experience of this election would show them that nothing bet a politi- cal dividing line would create such interest as had been manifested in that contest, and he hoped , that in the future it would be kept on those lines, and he had no learthat they would see Mr, Ocithston occupying-some honourable position in connection with the town. (Ap- plause.) He moved a vote of thanks to those who had worked so nobly in that election.—Mr. Norman en- dorsed what Mr. Handley had said, and remarked that there was no dOubt that the name of Hazlehurst was a power irrthe town, and a good nAny *ad gone over to the Major's side more out of sentiment than anything else. div.head: TRIAL AND SENTENCE OF MRS. OSBORNE. ' At the Old Bailey, on Wednesday morning, Mr
div.p: THE TRIAL AND SENTENCE OF MRS. OSBORNE. ' At the Old Bailey, on Wednesday morning, Mr
Florence Ethel Osborne was charged for perjury in her sensational action for libel against Major and

Mrs. Hargreave in connection with the sensational robberyofp earls from the house ofthe latter. As when the case was heard at Bow-st., ladies were present in 'great numbers. Captain Osborne was early in at- tendance,and took his seat in the well of the court behind counsel, and immediately opposite the jury- box, beneath which Major and Mrs. Hargreave very shortly afterwards took up their position. There was an extraordinarly strong array of counsel, many of the juniors being unable to find places on their own benches. Mr. Forrest Fauton, Q.C., M.P. appeared to prosecute, while the prisoner was re- presented by Sir Charles Russell, Q.C.. M.P., Mr. Matthews, Q.C., and Mr. Lewis Coward. Mr. Jus- tice Smith took his seat at. 10-30, by which hour even the gangways of the court were completely blocked by junior counsel. Mrs. Osborne, dressed in black, as at the preliminary trial, was supported into the dock by a female warder, whose arm, passed round her waist, served in some measure to support her. She looked terribly worn and wan, and sobbed convulsively, and was evi- dently in a state of semi-collapse. The clerk of the court at once read over the charge of .theft, and asked her to greed. In a voice that was only just -audible in the silent court she replied "Guilty." The question was repeated with respect to the I charge of perjury, but this time the answer could not be heard at all a few feet away, and what the prisonerhad said could only be conjectured until the warder beside her repeated "Guilty, sir. Mr. Fulton, Q.C., who represented the Public Pros- ecutor, explained that the prisoner's crime would have been left to be dealt with by private persons but for the fact that by her perjury she had at- tempted to interfeie with the due course of law and justice. Sir Charles Russell made an appeal for mercy on behalf of the prisoner, which was sup- ported by Mrs. Hargreave in a voice broken with emotion. Mr. Justice Smith, in passing sentence, said that but for the interposition of the person who made it possible at the, slander trial to produce the bank note bearing the prisoner's endorsement. Major and Mrs. Hargreave would have left the court with the stain of indelible ignominy upon them. The maximum penalty for perjury was seven years' penal servitude, but tak- ing into consideration various circumstances of the case, he should pass sentence of nine months' im- prisonment onlwith such hard labour as thestate of the prisoners's health would permit. Mrs. Osborne, who had wept bitterly during the whole of the roceedings, seemed astounded at the sentence, and di immediately into a state of almost complete collapse. She was promptly carried by the warders and wardresses to the cells below. Both Captain Osborne and Mrs. Hargreave were deeply affsctel

div.head: GLASS TRADE OF ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE GLASS TRADE OF ST. HELENS.

REDUCTION OF WAGES. St. Helens is not only seriously affected by the threatened stoppage of colliers, but for a consider- able time past the plate glass trade--fone of the staple industries of the town—has been, and is at present, passing through a severe crisis. Reference has been made on several occasions to the fact that the keen foreign competition experienced by the English plate-glass makers has compelled the local manufac- turers to commence extensive alterations to their works as well as provide for the introduction of the newest and best glass-making maehinery. The alterations have, to some extent, interfered with the conditions under which the workmen, have been employed. A week or two ago the Union Plateglass pompany's ' works at Pocket Nook were closed, and some 500 men were thrown out of employment owing to a failure in negotia- tion§ with the workmen, an.d it is expected that nti work will be found for the majority of the men during the next nine or twelvt, rannths—the period whictf will elapse before the structural alterations ,now in progress have been completed. This fact alone has been considered to be a bad thing for. the prosper- ity of the town, but some excitement was occasioned ,n Saturday by a rumour that the extensive firm Of the London and Manchester Plate Glass Com- pany, whose works are at Sutton and RaVenhead, had decided to reduce the wages of their workpeople. In- quiries have elicited that the report was well founded. Tiae London and Manchester Plate Glass Company find employment for about 1,000 men, 140 women, Sod 300 young,persons, and, last week posted notice... 4 intimating that in anticipation of a scarcity of fuel, the services of all persons in their employ, with the exception of a cer- tain number retified to the contrary, would be dis- spensed • with after Wednesday night. In accordance with the eipressed wish of the manager, Mr. Binney, a deputation of the workmen representative of every de- partment of the works waited upon that gentleman at , the offices of the C .mpany, at Sutton, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. Sinney, in the course of con- versation with the men, explained to them that the . firm could not afford to pay the present prices asked for supplies of coal, and it was found necessary to tempor- arily close the works. Be also intimated that when the works were reopened the men would have to submit to a reduction in their wages. It is stated that Mr. Binney did not say what the amount of reduction in the wages of men would be, and the men did not ask the question. The subject was brought before a meeting of the execu- tive committee of the United Plate Glass Workers' Association, held at the Flesketh Arms, Church-street, St. Helens, on Saturday night, hut owing to the lack of official. information on the matter its consideration was left Over for a special meeting. Messrs.Pilkington Bros.' Glass Works are in full swing, and there does not appear to he any probability that the I pvesent.position of affairs will materially interfere with their works. •

div.head: WORKING FOR MINERALS UNDER CANALS. IMPORTANT DECISION.
div.p: WORKING FOR MINERALS UNDER CANALS. IMPORTANT DECISION.

in the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Kekewich deliver- ed his reserved judgment in the action of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company v. Evans and Co., which was one of an injunction to restrain the defendants from working the minerals under and adjacent to plaintiffs' canal, which is known as the Sankey Canal, and for damages. Sir Henry James, Q.C., and Mr. 0. Leigh Clare, instructed by Mr. Mason, of Easton, appeared for the plaintiffs; and Sir Horace Davy, Q.C., Mr. Rigby, Q.C., Mr. jtenshaw,_Q.C., and Mr. Warrington, instructed by Mr. W. 11. Brook, of Warrington, appeared for the -defendants, His Lordship said a common law rig!)t to sup- port was a right to property based on tha natural claim of every man to enjoy his own undisturbed by others, whether neighbours or strangers. - The statement of claim insisted upon the support' of the canal only by sibjacent soil, and such adjacent soil as at a particular date was vested in persons owners of land in or over which the canal was constructed. The real question was 'whether a grant by the Act of George IL of a right to make and maintain a canal, be it styled an- easement or not, carried with it the right to prevent the grantors, meaning thereby the landowners on whose behalf the Legislature made the grant, from wOrking minerals to the detriment of the canal. What the defendants were at liberty to do, and' to what liabilities, if any, they might subject them- selves, if they worked their minerals so as to destroy the canal, he did not, because he need not, determine. 'What he held was that the'plaintiffs were not entitled to the injunction asked for. Their claim failed, and there must be judgment for the defendants with costs.

RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the HALF-YEAR ENDING IST OCTOBER, 1892.

The Guardians of the poor of the Runcorn Union, a.e desirous of receiving TENDERS from parties willing to contract for the supply of new milk, buttermilk, fresh butter, and fresh eggs, (for twelve months); flour, oat- meal, groceries, peas, cheese, salt butter ; cod liver and paraffin oil ; quinine ; good beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price include about 401bs. per week of the best butchers meat for the Officers, and sides of mutton ; home cured bacon ; potatoes ; wheat straw ; drapery and clothing ; men's women's, boys', and girls' shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton ; house coal (colliery to be named); good deal coffins, specify- ing size and including plate with name, age, and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required ; carting at per mile, funerals at per funeral. Parties Tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned Goods, will be required to deliver the same at the Work- house, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with Samples (except Drapery Goods), as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any Tender. Persons desirous of Tendering, must apply by letter, to my office. in Runcorn, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's Office, Runcorn, on or before Saturday, the 19th day of March, 1892, endorsed "Tender for The Tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board-room, Dutton, on the 22nd day of March, 1892, at two p.m. Parties whose Tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be pre- pared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians.—By order of the Board, JOHN ASHTON, Clerk to the Guardians. Buncona, Ist March, 1892.

remarks that— " The exhortations to Londoners to wake up and look after their affairs have not been Without effect, but they have reached the wrong People." No; "not the wrong people," for they have reached the people; it has been a struggle between the masses and the classes, with the usual result, when the masses are roused, in that the Glasses have had to go to the wall. London is crifficult to stir ; and it is a matter of course to say that when London is awake the whole of the gountry is awake. It really comes to this—that the enfranchised from one end of the kingdom to the other desire to see something come of their voting. The franchise is nothing to the workers • Szeapt as a means to an end; and they perceive that that end—which is to better their lot in life— oltu only be attained by supporting the Progressive Sr Liberal party.

Statesman HANDBOOKS of facts and figures 's Year-book have a tendency to multiply in these days of specialisation and Classification; but " The Statesman's Year-book," Published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., stands atelle as a statistical and historical annual which "ers the whole world. It was apparent from the first that it had come: to stay, and, as the 'velum° for 1892 is the twenty-ninth publication, it is a matter of course to say that it is well estab- lialleci. The work is edited by Mr. J. Scott Keltie, Librarian to the Royal Geographical Society, who has unrivalled sources of information, and spares 4° pains to ensure accuracy and bring everything UP to date. This year the publication has been a°, nlevuhat delayed in order that the results of the leading censuses of the world might be incorpor- ated; but, this having been accomplished, it is °hvious that the work is this year of more than ordinary value for purposes of reference. The re- 'bled estimate of the population of the world for 1.890 is 1,467,920,000,which gives 29 persons to the at(lllare mile upon an area of 51,250,800 square miles. It is worth noting that the value of gold and silver in tho different countries of the world is 11,572,414,000 which is, roundly speaking, £1 per- ▪ for every person in the world. This does not °f course bear any relation to the total wealth of !Ile World. Turning to the United Kingdom, with • total population of 37,888,153, we observe that When the census was taken, on April sth last year, there were 62 owns in England and Wales with alere than 50,000 inhabitants. The average increase °f Population in these towns from 1881 to 1891 Wa 14.2 per cent. The smallest growth is that of • tb—from 51,814 to 51,843, an increase of 0.1 • cent. ;while the largest growth is that of Lay- from 27,026 in 1881 to 63,106 in 1891, an increase of 133.5 per cent. St. Helens and War- rington have grown, in the same period, at much Cire than , the average rate ; St. Helens from i 403 to 71,288 (increase 24.2) and Warrington from 42,552 to 52,742 (increase 23.9 per cent.) 15Ile growth of Wigan has been from 48,194 to bt,1313, or 14.1 per cent., which is a fraction 401ely the, average of towns with more than ,000 inhabitants. We have had occasion to !°llllllent of late upon the decrease of population 11 Ireland. In 1891 it contained only three cities with over 50,000 inhabitants, namely, Dublin with 24,7Q9 but 361,891 within the metropolitan tlice district ; Belfast 255,896; and Cork 75,070. 3 reerick has 37,072 inhabitants, Londonderry t'B93, and Waterford 21,693. It should be men- -I°lled that in one respect Ireland is an example to theN,; rest of the United Kingdom. In England and Wales the proportion of illegitimate births to the ..A1 births in 1890 was 4.6; in Scotland it was as high as 7.5, while in Ireland for 1889—the latest v,ll-lePlete record—it was 2.8 per cent. only. It 01 be seen therefore that, in proportion to popu- Ireland has only half the number of illegiti- Zte children compared with the rest of the tellgdona—a fact which should be thrown in the tit:th of the Tories of the Salisbury type who are Pc'eed to compare Irishmen to Hottentots and cribe them as uncivilised. But, to return to the aar-book, it should be stated that a new feature . introduction of maps relating to subjects of tie"ent interest, namely, the ;density of popula- t of the globe; the distribution of the British InDire • the partition of Africa; and the inter- natic nal frontiers on the Pamirs. There is a full e; which enables the reader to readily get at vol'rreation as to every country in the world; the Ixtl4ee is one of 1,150 pages; it is handsomely ; and the price is half a guinea.

div.p: " TOUCII AND GO."
S. N. Green.—Your letter on the half-holiday question reached us too late for this week.

The Warrington town clock has been stopped, but not like "My Grandfather's Clock" "never to go again"; for it has simply been undergoing Blight repair. It was "on tick" again on Wednes- day, and will continue to keep, it is expected, the remarkably good time for which it is noted.

Widnes is about to have a permanent henne for its Technical Schools. Arrangements are being made with the Local Board for the erection of a new Library building; and the Technical Institute will be built in conjunction with it. This, it is anticipated, will be a happy unior. ; it certainly promises well.

Mr. 11. J. Farmer Atkinson, M.P. for Boston, has gone raving mad at Nice, and been placed in an asylum. It was evident that there was some- thing wrong with him when he created scenes in the House of Commons; and the members seemed to be aware of it, for he was treated with great leniency.

The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority will do well not to be to a few pounds in settling their Clerk's salary if, as is understood, he is not to charge anything for legal work. It will be better in the end both for them and him. "It is not and it cannot come to good " when the Clerk of any Authority has an interest in litigation.

In another column there *ill be found the first portion of an interesting communication from Mr. H. Whitham, who, having left San Francisco, crossed the American continent, and pitched his tent near Worcester,Mass.,is giving his experience of life under new conditions. It will be seen that the picture is by no means flattering to San Fran- cisco.

It must be set down to another of Mr. Goschen's failures that he has not put himself in a position to accept the offer of Mr. Tate to erect a gallery for British Art, on a suitable site being provided. A suitable site would cost something; and the Chancellor of the Exchequer cannot find the money. How is it? Is there going to be a deficit this year?

The return of a Liberal for South Derbyshire with an increased majority, and the magnificent success of the Liberals in the London County Council elections have been as bad as the weather to the Tories; it has made them shake in their shoes. There is no talk now of an early dissolu- tion; they mean to drag on as long as they can ; but, as the unexpected sometimes happens, Liberals should worg as if the elections might be upon them next month.

Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Limited, can- not as yet be said to feel the need of making a reduction in colliers' wages, for at the third ordin- ary general meeting held the other day, it was reported that the net profit for the year was £65,008 7s. id. It was resolved that the dividend should be 0,..e of 8 per cent; and that £lO,OOO should be placed to the reserve fund. £lO,OOO will do ; it is a nice egg to add to the others in the nest.

Coal is King now and a merry old soul is he, for isn't everybody bending the knee to him P It is a good time for colliery proprietors, who are clear- ing out their stocks at an advance in many cases of over 50 per cent., and that, too, before the strike ! Indeed, if they had paid the men to bring about the present situation, it couldn't, thus far, have suited them better. Their pirch may come when their works stop—though if the stoppage be a short one, they will not mind it. The chief suflerers are the public who are wondering how long the fleecing process is to last.

The Government were defeated by a majority of 238 to 119, on Wednesday, on the Places of Worship Enfranchisement Bill. Mr. Balfour tried to smother the measure by referring it, along with other bills, to a Select Committee; but even some of his own supporters could not stand this trans- parent device; they, therefore, voted for the bill with the result that the Government were routed. Still, they will not resign ; they mean to wait until they are as badly beaten at the polling booths.

It was the turn of the Salvationists to triumph on Thursday. The bill for the repeal of the ob- noxious clause in the Eastbourne Improvement Act under which the Corporation have maltreated a section of their fellow-townsmen, passed the second reading in the House of Commons by a majority of 147. The clause ought never to have been sanctioned,for it is distinctly at variance with the ordinary law of the land; and, more than that, has been brutally and illegally enforced. But it is to be repealed; and the rights of meeting and pro- cession will be maintained.

The Emperor of Germany is making himself ridiculous by showing himself excessively sensitive to criticism ; and, more than that, he is acting tyrannically in ipstituting press prosecutions for such oftences as re-producing an article from the London "Times." If he will persist upon being to the front as lord of all, and of making his policy' a personal matter, he must accept what neces- sarily comes of it—personal criticism. If he is in the right, he will benefit by the discussion of his projects; if wrong, the sooner he is set right the better. He will certainly come a cropper if lie sits on the safety valve.

Great is the force of habit. Some 300 soldiers of the 17th Bengal Infantry were in the thick of a row with natives in Calcutta when, we are told, "in the very height of the tumult the mere sound- ing of a bugle in the barracks summoning the men to return caused the riot to collapse." In harmony with this automatic action is the way in which deserters are sometimes " spotted " by the police. When a suspect is seen, the constable who can get behind him whilst walking suddenly calls out " Halt l" If the man has been in the army, he is almost sure to make some movement in response, and thus betrays himself—if a deserter.

As was to be expected, pestilence is on the heels of the famine in Russia. The news to hand is that —"Hunger-typhus has now broken out with great virulence in nearly all the famine-stricken govern- ments. The mortality amongst the peasantry is terrible. In many districts containing thousands of people there are neither doctors, nurses, nor medicine." It would appear as if there are about to be realised the horrors of the calamity which fell upon Ireland in 1846-47, when over a million lives were lost through lack of timely assistance; when "whole families perished unvisited and unas- sisted ;" and when "by levelling above their corpses the shealing in which they died, the neighbours gave them a grave."

Savage or civilized, your human biped will wear rings; and Tennyson, in "Maud," hits the mark with a suggestive allusion when he says:— I noticed one of his many rings, For he had many, poor worm. "Poor worm" is decidedly good, seeing that the worm is a creature of rings. Miss Fanny Noon, a London barmaid, is also a creature of rings, for she was wearing five when she was induced by a visitor to the bar, who was a perfect stranger to her, to take two off by way of convincing him that they were "real gold." Result: one ring was returned and the other was missing; a policeman was called in; a magistrate has heard the evidence, and the stranger is committed for trial. Fanny will perhaps content herself with four rings for the future, and be a little less vain about showing them to strangers, who are not always angels in disguise.
CHEMICAL WORKERS AND THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

Mr. P. J. King, of St. Helens, president of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, on Wednes- day morning received a communication from Mr. Geoffrey Drage, secretary of the Royal Commission on Labour, stating that he had been directed by the chairman of committee "C" of the commission to invite him to give evidence on Friday, March 18. Mr. King was asked to forward at once two copies of a summary of the evidence he proposed to offer.
