div.p: Sr. AMBROSE. MISSION .Roog, .WIDNES..

The monthly meeting of the adult branch of St. Ambrose Church Temperance Society, was held on Tuesday night, under the presidency of Mr. George Rae. An excellent programme of music was gone through. g&UmraumLes ItEcovnaEn.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT PEERS' ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY.

The Bth ballot of the above Society was held at their offices, on Monday evening, Mr. J. H. Annett presiding, schen No. 164 was drawn, entitling Miss Strong to an advance of £5OO for 161 years without interest. PRINCES-STREET CHAPEL, WIDNES. _ "

On Wednesday evening, a service' of song, entitled "Little Abe," was given at the above chapel, by the members of the Halton-road Band of Hope, Runcorn. Mr. Walter Brown, (Ditton), occupied the chair, and Mr. A. E. Calvert read the various parts.

OXFORD UNIVERSITY LECTURE AT RUNCORN. The fifth lecture of the series on Florentine History was held on Monday in Bethesda School, by the Rev.W. Hudson Shaw, who dealt with the life and career of Machiavelli. The lecture was illustrated by limelight views shown by Mr. 11. W. Handley. ACE-BRAND SPIDER.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge-st., Warrington. ELECTION OF GUARDIANS TO RUNCORN UNION.

From particulars supplied by the Relieving Officer (Mr. Ashton) it appears that nominations must be handed in between the 14th and 26th inst. to the return- ing officer or to the relieving officers of the several districts. Shonld there be a contest voting papers will be delivered on April Bth, collected on the following day and counted on the 11th. TUN BRUTAL ASSAULT AT WIDNES.

At Liverpool County Intermediate Sessions on Wed- nesday before Mr. Hugh Perkins, chairman, Sir W. B. Forwoed, and a bench of magistrates, James M`Camley, (27), labourer, was charged with having at Widnes, on the 6th ult.' unlawfully wounded Jane Oliver, with intent to do her grevious bodily harm, by kicking her with heavy clogs.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to nine months' hard labour. BASSINETTES. - Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Earlestown.

div.head: RUNCORN GREENWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS.
div.p: RUNCORN GREENWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS.

Mr. J. F. Moulton, the headmaster, has recently com- menced a monthly magazine in connection with this school, and it is highly popular amongst the young people. From this month's number we take the follow- ing item :—" The Girls' School Library has been aug- mented by 21 volumes,which have been obtained partly from a portion of the proceeds of the bazaar, held at Christmas, and partly by subscriptions from tho girls themselves." WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOL, WESTON.

On Tuesday evening a magic lantern entertainment was given in aid of the funds of the ab we school. The subject of the views was the " Land of the Rose, Sham- rock, and the Thistle," including a number of pictures of places of local interest. The slides were thrown upon the screens by a lime-light lantern, mani- pulated by Mr. Epps, assisted by Mr. John Ball, the for- mer of whom also described the views, which were greatly appreciated by the numerous company present.

div.head: _ BUILDING OPERATIONS IN WIDNER.
div.p: _ BUILDING OPERATIONS IN WIDNER.

At the monthly meeting of Widnes Local Board on Tuesday, the Highways Committee reported that they had dealt with the following plans submitted by the Surveyor :—Temporary Mission Room in Davies-st • for the Rev. G. H. Garrett ; new schools in Widnes, for the Rev. G. H. Garrett. approved ; 22 houses in Denton-st., for Edwin Woods, disapproved ; estate plan showing Denton-st., for Edwin Woods, disapproved ; 4 villas in Deacon-road for Messrs. Sayce and Randle, approved ; bank in Albert-st., for Parr's Banking Company, dis- approved. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. ST/EALING A BASSINETTE AT WIDNES. George Hayes, of St. Helens, was brought up at Wid- nes Police Court on Tuesday to answer a charge of steal- ing a bassinette worth 305., the property of Frederick Jordan of Birchfield-road. On Monday evening Mrs., Jordan left the carriage on the footpath of Widnes-road while she entered a shop. On her return the carriage had disappeared and it was proved that the prisoner had taken it into the Albert Hotel on the same evening.—The prisoner was remanded until the Petty Sessions on Thursday, when he was fined 103. and costs. He stated in mitigation, that he committed the theft under the influence of a spree. THE NUISANCES OF. WIDNES.

Mr. Walter Lowe, nuisance inspector to Widnee Local Board has submitted his annual report for 1891. Among other matters it states that fifteen pounds weight of un- sound mutton exposed for sale was seized and destroyed by order of a magistrate. A diseased cow suffering from paralysis was killed and secretly conveyed and offered for sale in a neighbouring township,l 'elegraphed the inspector there, who had it seized and destroyed. 32ilbs. of beef and mutton, 3165. of cooked meat, 56Ibs. of pickled beef, 5271b5. of apples and pears, 1,325 oranges, (albs. of onions, and Nibs. of plums have also been destroyed. Prosecution for milk adulteration none.
SAFETY BICYCLE.—J. S. Garland. 51, Bridge-at., War- rington.
ROBBERY FROM A RUNCORN SCHOONER.

Thomas Piggott, a youth, was brought before Malor Hazlehurst and Mr. Henry Reynolds, at Runcorn Police Court, on rhursday, charged with stealing a sovereign belonging to Robert Lloyd Foulkes, mate of the schooner Annie Crosfield. The prisoner, who was a hand on the vessel, abstracted the money from the mate's trousers and decamped, but was captured at the railway station by P.C. Benfield. He had booked for Liverpool,but said he was on his way to London to see his parents. It transpired that he was one of Dr. Barnardo's shoeblacks. The Bench were unwilling to convict the prisoner, and bound him over to be of good behaviour for six months, and gave him a warning.
A HUSBAND'S INTERFERENCE AND THE RESULT._

At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Elizabeth Stapleton was charged with unlawfully wounding her husband David Stapleton of 9, Charlotte-street. On Monday night Mrs. Stapleton was chastising one of the children for coming home late, when her husband pro- tested and interfered and struck her. She retorted by throwing an earthenware cup at him, the missile striking the hand he put up to shield himself with, making a lacerated wound four inches long and severing several small arteries; and Dr. Olieeffe had to put four stitches in the wound.—Mr. Timmis : Do you wish your wife punished—Defendant : Not badly, because there are some children that want looking after.—The magistrate discharged the prisoner and warned her not to give way to such a violent temper in future. WIFE DESERTION AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. C. Reynolds, and Mr. H. Reynolds, at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Edward James Waterson of 8, Mersey-road, Widnes, was summoned for neglecting and deserting his wife Emma and two chil- dren. The complainant said two years ago the defendant broke his leg, and since then he had lived with his parents, who had a branch post office at Widnes, and kept him to assist in the shop. She had promised to maintain herself and one of the children if he would do the same, but he declined. She had been compelled to give up her house in Wellington-st., through being in arrears with her rent.—The defendant contended that his wife left him, and while he was in the hospital she broke up the hotne. He had been out of work since, but would keep the children as soon as he was able.— Mr. C. Reynolds: As soon as you are made. You will have to pay 6s. ,a weck for the maintenance of the child- ren and pay the costs of the order_, 10s. 6d. UMBRELLASRECOVILRED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Bankey-st., Warrington.— Advt.

div.head: NER. SATUR Y, MARCH 12, 1892.
div.p: NER. SATUR Y, MARCH 12, 1892.

WESTON BIBLE AND MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. The usual weekly meeting of this class was held on Monday night last, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, when a paper on "Man's relation to his Maker" was read by Mr. James Ford.
FUNERALS AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday afternoon Mrs. Annie Birkett, wife of John Birkett of Salisbury-Street, was ihterred in Runcorn Cemetery. Mrs. Birkett had only attained 27 years of age, and a demonstration of a symyath- tic character was made. The coffin was borne to the grave side on the shoulders of Messrs. W. T. Millington, H. W. Handley, R. Morton, A. Matthews, 1 H. Hughes, and E. Eden and walking in possession in front were the Rev. T. Wilkes, the Rev. W. Arrow- smith, Dr. Robinson, Messrs. J. Unsworth, R. Abel, W. Massey, .1. F. Moulton, Charles Littler and the members of St. Paul's Choir. The mourners were Messrs. J. Birkett, A. Hayes, R. B. Musgrove, A. Moore, J. Birkett, sea., R. Birkett, aad Masters Elwyn and Ernest Birkett. The Rev. W. Arrawsimith conducted the service in the chapel and the Rev, T. Wilkes at the grave side, where the choir sang " Wire me ways of faith to rise." Wreaths had been sent by Mr. J. Birkett, Mrs. Musgrove, Miss Carry Littler, Mr. J. Rhodes, Mrs. Abel, Mrs. Moss and St. Paul's choir. 1

On Sunday afternoon the remains of Mr. Thomas Dun- bavand, aged 47 years of Trentham-st., Runcorn, were interred in Runcorn Cemetery. The deceased, who was a master mariner' was a native of the town, and was highly respected by the sea-faring community. In September last he navigated his schooner "Countess of Garrick," to Swansea, where he became seriously ill and was taken to the Hospital, where he died on the Ist inst. His body was conveyed to Runcorn, and was followed , to its last resting place by about 100 relatives, friends, , and sea men. The funeral was conducted by the Rev. Thos. Wilks, (wesleyan), and Mr. W. Shaw (missionary), was present. The funeral of Mr. James Shaw, aged 52, of 31, Bold- street, Runcorn. took place on Sunday. The deceesed who had succumbed after an illness extending over three months, was held in great esteem by his fellow. workmen at the Old Copper W.orks, and had held an honourable position amongst the Odilfellows of the town. He had occupied the position of Secretary to the Star of Freedom Lodge, G.U.O. for about thirty years and for the past twenty year he had also acted as District Secretary, and about 120 Oddfellews paid the last mark of respect to their departed brother by form- ing part of the funeral eortege along with his fellow- workmen. The widow and children and relatives fol- lowed the hearse. A number of be Autiful wreaths were placed on the coffin.
OPENING OF A WESLEYAN CHAPEL AT DITTON.

On Sunday, the opening services were held in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, which has recently been erected in Steward's-lane, Ditton. The building,which is of corrugated iron, is situated in the centre of the viilage. and fronts the main thoroughfare. It is calculated to seat about 300 persons. The chapel formerly belonged to a party of Baptists, in Liverpool, and was purchased from them at a cost of £llO. A small vestry, /sc., has been erected at the back, and it is estimated that when complete, the cost of the building will be something like £250. The site was purchased some time ago from the late Mr. J. Hunt, for £lBO, which makes a total cost of £4lO. Although there is a population of almost 1,000 in the village, there was, until recently, no place of wor- ship whatever. This was greatly deplored by two or three local Wesleyans, but they found it WAS impractic- able to erect a chapel at the time, so that Mr. S. Sadler, Chestnut Lodge, offered to place a large room over one of the outbuildings at his residence, which was capable of seating 100 persons, at their disposal for the purpose of conducting religious services. The offer was gladly accepted, and from the crowded congregations it soon became evident that a larger building was required. This resulted in the purchase of the present chapel. Great praise is due to Mr. Herbert Neild for the untiring and earnest manner in which he has worked in behalf of this cause. The services on Sunday were conducted by the Rev. R. Burdon, who preached two eloquent and stirring sermons. In the evening a large number accepted the invitation to go to the penitent form. The morning con- gregation was very large, but in the evening the place was packed to excess, many being onable to gain admission. The singing, which was conducted by Mr. Nield, was exceptionally hearty. The collection amounted to £l6. On Monday evening a public tea meeting was held when about 300 sat down to an excellent tea. The after proceedings were presided over by Mr. J. Midwood who delivered an appr >priate address, and Mr. H. M. Neild submitted the financial statement. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. W. Pritchard, and the Rev. R. Burdon, and Mr. B. Brown. The collections realised £9, and promises amounting to £4O were made. On Tuesday evening 200 children were given a free tea.

div.head: TRANSFER OF LICENSES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TRANSFER OF LICENSES AT RUNCORN.

The Runcorn magistrates have granted the transfer of the following licenses :—Royal Oak, Weston, from Mr. William Green deceased, to his widow, Alice M. Green ; Wilsons Hotel;Bridge-street, from George W. Cooper, to Charles Dutton : Clarendon Hotel, Church-street, from Fanny Lea to Thomas White ; Norton Arms, Hatton, from G. E. Turley to Charles Birch • Nelson Inn, Run- corn, from William Dunbavand to George B. Jones, and Bird in Hand, Halton-road, from Samuel Price to Charles Thomas Bridgeman.
UMBRELLAS RECOTEIED.—.7. and W. Durrow, Sankey-Bt., Warrington.—Adot.
RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday after- noon, under the presidency of Mr. H. Coleburn, and there were present Messrs. W. Mellor, T. Handler, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The report stated that dur- ing the eleven months ending February 25th, there were 484 deaths,last year 448; increase 36. The fees received during the same period amounted to £416 6s. Bd. ; last year £409 15s. 10d. ; increase £6 10s. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of , accounts 'amounting to £2O 19s. 3d., and interest falling due on I loans to the amount of £67 N. Bd. The committee also recommended that the tender of Mr. T. J. Kirkham for grave coverings be accepted. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Mellor.—The Secretary was in- structed to negotiate a loan of £534 N. Bd. at 3i per cent, to pay for the making and sewering of Victoria- read. It was also resolved to serve a precept upon the overseers for £6O on Sinking Fund Account for the en- suing half-year. The question of grave-digging, &c., was deferred until the next meeting. ST. HELEN'B NEW RAILWAY.

The directors of the Liverpool, St. Ifelens. and South Lancashire Railway have decided to at once call up £20,000 more capital. The work is at pre- sent being rapidly pushed forward. FAILURE OF A ST. HELENS CONTRACTOR.

A meeting of the creditors of Mr. .John contractor for the Corporation intercepting sewer, was held on' Tuesday at the Fleece Hotel. Mr. Massey, solicitor, explained that the unsecured creditors amounted to £3,540, and the secured to £49. Mr. Riddell accounted for his failure he the Preston Banking Company accepting £2,500 in settlement of his claim of £B,OOO against the Sr. Helens Corporation for extras in connection with the sewer. Most of the creditors were in favour of accepting a composition, but Mr. Berry, of Liver- pool, contractor's merchant, whose claim amounted to £2,500, insisted on Riddell going through the Bankruptcy Court, and this was decided upon.

div.head: INQUEST AT . HOLLINFARE.
div.p: INQUEST AT . HOLLINFARE.

Last evening week an inquest was held on the body of the man, nicknamed " Scanni at the Boat- house, liollinfare. The coroner was Mr. Brighouse. From the evidence given, the man was found early on the Wednesday morning in a sluice,in close prox- imity to Rixton cutting. A deep wound was on the right side of the head, and a terrible wound in the mouth, which had been caused by falling on a spike. When found he was head downwards, the water in the drain being about nine inches deep. The jury, after considering the case, brought in a verdict of accidzintal death. The deceased lived at the huts situated on the banks of the canal. his name could not be ascertained. The body was in- terred on Saturday.

div.head: ENDANGERING COLLIERS' LIVES AT BOLD.
div.p: ENDANGERING COLLIERS' LIVES AT BOLD.

On Tuesday, at St. Helens Town Hall, Thomas Williams, a collier,-employed by the Collins Green Colliery Company at their Bold Colliery, was charged with a breach of the Coal Mines Regula- tion Act by unramming a shot which had misfired. Mr. Forshaw, solicitor, Warrington, prosecuted. It appeared that one of the shots used for . basting coal down the mine had failed to explode, and, con- trary to the regulations, the defendant had on- rammed it. Mr. Forshaw stated that the unram- ming of explosives was an extremely dangerous act, and an explosion would probably have resulted in defendant's death, as well as seriously endangered the lives of all the colliers in the pit. Defendant, who pleaded that he unrammed the shot very care- fully, was fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: IRON TRADE.
div.p: THE IRON TRADE.

Very little change has taken place in the English iron market during the past week ; business is re- stricted to hand-to-mouth requirements, and on every side notices to close works in consequence of the miners' stoppages are being exhibited. The Cleveland market remains in an unsettled condition, with prices exceedingly irregular, and in all other pig-iron centres trade is very quiet. Manufactured iron is in limited enquiry, and tinplates remain dull. The steel trade shows little alteration. The rail branch is neglected, and the Board of Trade returns just issued exhibit a deplorable falling-off in the quantity of railway material exported, which amounted to only 18,402 tons, a decrease on February 1891 of 37,350 tons. Shipbuilding shows no change since our last report. Engineers are getting slacker. The coal trade is still active prior to:the suspension of work.—lron. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF A VETERAN PREACHER.

On Monday afternoon, at Sr. Mary's Churchyard, Lowton, one of the oldest and best respected of the inhabitants of Lowton was interred, in the person of Mr. Jas. Eckersley, of Mather-lane, Lowton. Mr. Eckersley, whose death took place on the Thursday evening, had attained the ripe age of 88 years. The deceased had been a local Independent Methodist since he attained the age of about 16 years, and on many occasions had preached three times in one day. Besides preaching in Lowton, he had also preached at Golborne, Warrington, Bolton, and other large towns, and always attracted large con- gregations. Previous to the interment, a short ser- vice was held in the Lowton Independent Methodist Chapel, after which the burial rites were performed by the Rev. W. Berridge. M.A., vicar of St. Mary's. Deceased was well known and highly respected by old and young, and his funeral was attended by about 130 villagers.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL STUDENTS.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL STUDENTS.

The report of the Liverpool Diocesan Inspector, the Rev. Joseph Pulliblank, for the year 1891 has just been published, and contains the following para- graph :—" In the December examination, especially on the results of which your lordship's prizes are awarded, the number was so small that I questioned at first whether it would be right to award all the four prizes, but on looking over the papers sent in I have no hesitation in saying that whether among few candidates or among many, the following have so acquitted themselves as fully to deserve the dis- tinction which the Bishop's prize confers :-1, M. J. Smethurst, Hamilton-street School, Warrington ; 2, R. Dwerryhouse, St. Marv's,Widnes ; 3. L. M. Wilde, St. Margaret's, A nfield ; 4,P. E. ICiblott,St. Margaret's Anfield. All of these have previously gained dis- tinction, some of them for several years in succession in the first class at the annual general examination of the pupil teachers of the diocese." Miss Smethurst, mentioned above, is a daughter Councillor James Smethurst.

div.head: GLASS BOTTLE TRADE.
div.p: THE GLASS BOTTLE TRADE.

A week or two ago it was reported that the ex- tensive glass bottle firm of Messrs. Cannington,Shaw and Co., St. Helens, had arranged with their work- men to run their work oa short time owing to the warehouses being overstocked with bottles. Another lar:e firm 'n the town—that of Messrs. Nuttall and Co.—have been compelled to adopt a similar curtailm:nt of the hours of labour. Last week Messrs. Nuttall and Co. gave notice that in ( onseque ice of the unsettled stew of the coal trade the services of aeir employes would be dispensed with after the present week. The officials of the Lancashire Glass Bottle Makers' Trade Protection Asseciation have had an interview with Councillor Nu.tall, the head of the firm, and a mutual arrange- ment was come to that the men should work on the same conditions as those of Messrs. Cannington, Shaw. and Co. As a result of an agreement, the men will work in two shifts, playing one week and working the next. It is understood that this system will come into operation next week.—The direc- tors ot the London and Manchester Plate-glahs Co., have posted notices to the shareholders that in con- sequence of the great fall in the selling prices of plate glass they have decided not to issue the usual interim dividend ot 5 percent.

ROBBING A FATIIHR.—Marthe. Johnson, aged 17, of 75 Pear-st., pleaded guilty to stealing a table-cloth and a quantity of clothing, the property of her father, Peter Johnscn. EXTRAORDINARY ASSAM-T.—Witham Clare was sum- moned for asßaulting Henry Goodhead.—The men live together at 8 Terrace-road, and on the 4th inst. it was alleged, the defendant kicked Mrs. Goodhead and then struck complainant on the face, and also kicked him severely. div.head: WOMENS LIBERAL ASSOCIATION, WIDNES.
div.p: WOMENS LIBERAL ASSOCIATION, WIDNES.

The inauguration of a ‘Voinen's Liberal Association for Widnes, took place On Tnursday night i(I the Baths Assembly room and the proceedings were wtended with gratifying success. A business meeting was held at half past six, when a code of rules were adopted and it was decided to affiliate the Association with the Central Association, in London of which Mr. Gladstone is presi- dent. Afterwards about 400 persons sat down to tea, and then a public meeting was held under the presid- ency of Mr. E. Carey who was supported on the platform by a large number of ladies and Mr. H. Wade Deacon the Liberal candidate. There was a crowded audience. The Chairman said a Women's Liberal Association was something he had looked forward to in a kind of dream, but lie hardly expected to see it in reality during his lifetime, and that .fleeting had exceeded his greatest expectations. (Applause.) There were people who said women had no business to interfere in politics, but he contended that women had half of the burdens of life upon their shoulders. They were as much interested in the social and political welfare of the country as the men, and lie looked forward to the time when women would be enfranchised. Be heartily welcomed that Association and believed that it would do much to spread a know- ledge of Liberal principals and without descending to the methods of the Primrose League, assist at the next elec- tion in returning Mr. Deacon at the head of the poll. (Loud applause ) Miss Gould read the list of officers appointed as fol. lows :—President, Mrs. Stewart Brown; vice-presidents Mrs. Deacon, Mrs. Gossage, Mrs. Muspratt, Mrs. Gas- kell, Mrs. Timmis, Mrs Brunner, and Miss Snaps ; hon. treasurers, Mrs. O'Keeffe, and Miss Morrison ; hon. secs. Miss Carrie Deac)n, and Miss Hilda De.tcon ; literature secretary, Mrs. Robinson. Mrs. Stuart Brown, whom the Chairman introduced as the friend of their ot I friend Mr. E. R. Mu tpratt,received 'an enthusiastic reception. She thanked them for the honour they had conferred upon her in electing her as their first president. She knew that they had done so not because of her personal merit but because she was her father's daughter. (Applause.) At the last two elections she had worked for the Liberal candidates and she hoped to help their present candidate Mr. Wade- Deacon with better success, because the Irish were now united with the Liberal party, and the Liberal Unionists no longer existed as a party. (Applause.) As to the argument that women should not interfere in political affairs, she showed how deeply interested women were in many of the important social and political questions that were at present agitat- ing the country, and how they were intimately connected with a women's whole life. (Applause.) In conclusion she asked them for the sake of temperance, of justice to Ireland, for their own sakes and for the sake of the Liberal party and Mr. Gladstone let them come forth that night and join the association. (Applause.) Miss Riley, of Southport, then delivered an address and Mr. H. Wade-D .acon gave a chatty speech plan ap- propriate character. The usual votes of thanks were passed.

div.head: 'PRESOOT BOARD OF OIIA.RDIAI4B.
div.p: 'PRESOOT BOARD OF OIIA.RDIAI4B.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thursday afternoon, Mr. James Burchall presiding. There were also present Messrs. Tyrer, Johnson, lianas, Middlehurst, Goldsworth, }Con- wright, Daine, Graves, Wareing, Mercer, Lowe, Whalley, W. B. Longton. E. Syder, and A. T. Mann (clerk). WORKHOUSE INMATES—The workhouse master said there were 622 inmates in the house this week, 614 last week, and 573 in the corresponding week of last year. Outdoor relief had been given to 3,429 persons at a cost of £342 les. Id., against 3,384 persons at a cost of ' £213 13s. last week and 3,147 persons and £271 13s. sd. in corresponding week last year. IRE MASTER'S SALARY.—A letter was read from the , Local Government Board assenting to the proposal of the Guardians to increase the aalary of Mr. Arthur H. Hale, workhouse maater,from £l3O to £lBO per annum. TEE ALKALI CO. AND FOREIGN LABOUR.—The Clerk read the following letter:—" Widnes. March 10111,1892. Sir,—l have been deputed by the relief workers of Wid- nes, to bring the following statemont under the notice of your board at their meeting to- day (Thursday). At the present time and for some considerable time there has been employed in the Widnes Chemical Works a great number of Poles whilst we who are chiefly composed of householders and ratepayers are compelled to walk to and from Whiston daily for the purpose of keeping body and soul together. We shoold be very thankful to the Board if they would, through you communicate with the authorities of the Limited Alsali Company, to see if they can do anything in this matter as we think it strange they should consent to assist in supporting us here and at the same time pay complete strangers to the country for work that we should now be doing. We would not have troubled you with this statement only that we have been mis'ed so often by reports that the Poles were to be discharged to make ro.ml for us. Finding that this was only imagination on the part of someone we thought that we would see if th-. board could do anything in the matter, yours truly Joseph Nott."—lt was explained by the Clerk that the -Guardians could not interfere in the the matter.—Mr. 'Fyrer remarked that it was a fact that there were a great many people out of work and

yet foreigners were allowed to displace Englishmen.— Mr. Wareing said they wanted some legislation on the matter.—Mr. Tyrer : Sometimes we are asked to assist in emigration out of this country while there are thousands of foreigners corning in in a destitute condition and they would work for anything.—lt was ultimately decided that the clerk should write acknow- ledging receipt of the letter, and stating the the Guardians could not interfere ia the matter.

div.head: PRESCOT GUARDIANS ELECTION.
div.p: PRESCOT GUARDIANS ELECTION.

The period of three years for which the Guardians of the Prescot Union were last elected will expire early in April, and arrangements are being made for the election of a new board. All the retiring mem- bers are eligible for re-appointment. Nominations must be made on or before the 26th inst., and if a contest is necessary in any of the townships, voting papers will be delivered on the Bth April, and collected on the following day. It is generally thought that there will be very few, if any, changes. The retiring mem- bers are as follows :—Bold, Mr. J. R. Whalley; Crouton, Mr. W. B. Longton ; Ditton, Rev. C. W. div.head: TECHNICAL INSTITUTE FOR WIDNES.
div.p: THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE FOR WIDNES.

Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, adopted the following minutes of the General Purposes Com- mittee with regard to the Technical Instruction Schools and New Library :—The Clerk read the resolution of the Local Board with respect to the erection of a new library in connection with the Technical In- struction Schools and referring the matter thereof to this Committee with a view to their carrying out the arrangements in regard to the erection of such schools and library. Resolved that subject to arrangements be- ing completed for acquiring the proposed site the plan of the library building, prepared be' the Slrveyor and now produced and the cost of which he estimates at £2,000, be approved; and that the Clerk and Surveyor be authorised and instructed to make provision for such building in the instructions to the arcnitects as to competitive plans directed to be prepared by them with respect to the Technical Instruction School. Resolved that with a view to the more convenient carry- ing out of the arrangements for the erection of the said schools and library. the Technical Instruction Committee and the Library Committee be each requested to nomin- ate three of their members to form with this Committee a Special Committee for acquiring the land, obtaining , designs, and for the general carrying out of the works. The Library Committee have nominated Messrs. Deacon, Robinson, and W. Sadler, and the Technical Instruction Committee—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. K. Muspratt and W. J. Morrison to act in conjunction with the General Purposes Committee in this matter.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD ItUNCORNIA.N.
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD ItUNCORNIA.N.

Mr. William Bradbury, father of Mrs. Brimelow, the well-known greengrocer in Bridge-st., died on Tuesday last at the advanced age of 94 years, at his daughter's place of tusiness, and the " oldest in- habitant" may be said to have passed away. The deceased who was the son of a farmer, was born at Ince, in Cheshire, and was a man of iron constitu- tion and strong muscular development and had scarcely a day's illness in the whole of his long life, and his death was due not to any specific disease, but to natural decay. Up to two years ago he was able to read without the aid of glasses, and his other faculties more unimpaired. In fact so strong and healthy did he appear a few weeks ago that it seemed not improbable that he would reach the century. In his younger days the deceased was of a somewhat wild disposition and before he was 20 years of age he had enlisted as a soldier, deserted, enlisted again and been bought off. In those days too, the cup which not only cheers but also inebriates had its charm for him, and many were the stories he used to tell of the mad pranks played by him when under the influence of the "rosy wine." The temperance party were practically an unknown force in those days, but since he had been 40 years of age, Mr. Bradbury had been a staunch teetotaller, and whether this fact conduced to his longevity or not, it is impossible to say. It was in 1839 that Mr. Bradbury eaine to Run- corn, and atter a brief period of work under the Bridge- water Trust, he commenced business as a greengrocer, and he was actively engaged io bu.aineas until a few years ago. The funeral takes place at the cemetery on Sunday.

div.head: LICENSING PROSECUTIONS AT WIDNES.
div.p: LICENSING PROSECUTIONS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, the mag- istrates (Mr. J. Brock, and Lieut. Col. Gaskell) were engaged for several hours deciding prosecutions under the Licensing Acts. The first case was one in which Wm. O'Hagan, of the Crown Vaults, Ann- street West, was summoned for 'allowing gaming on his licensed premises an the night of the 24th February, and also NC ith selling intoxicating liquors during prohibited hours on the 25th ult.

div.head: I PATHETIC STORY.
div.p: I PATHETIC STORY.

Mr. T. Swift, (barrister), instructed by Mr. Knowles, defended, and said he did not intend to con- test the question of playing cards. Defendant took charge of the premises simply to support the six orphan children of the previous licensee, who was a relative of O'Hagan's, and also to maintain a young woman named Miss O'Hagan, who was dying from consumption. The landlc .1 and three men were playing at cards for half- pennies, but altogether they had not lost more than 6d. and the offence was committed in ignorance, the three men being his invited guests for the night. If the de- fendant were convicted he would be turned out ot the house, the dying woman would be sent to the work- house, and the orphan children would be left to the mercy of the world. He trusted that with the sanction of the Bench the police would withdraw the charge.— Supt. Beighley refused to do this, and P.S. .McCracker deposed that half an hour after midnight on the 23rd February he went to the rear of the vaults, and through ths kitchen window which had no blind, he saw the defendant and three men named Patrick Healey, and John Elkes, both af 8, Fredrick- street, Widnes ; and Martin Healey, of Burnley, plaOng a game of cards called banker. He saw money pass and there were glasses of liquor on the table. Inspector Pattiminn was present, and knocked at the front door, when Patrick Healey put the cards in his pocket and the glasses were cleared away. The landlord said the men were his guests.—ln defence, Mr. Swift said the liquor was given and not sold.—The Bench considered the case of gaming proved and imposed a fine of 40s. and costs and the charge of selling liquor was dismissed on payment of costs.—The other men for aiding and abet- ting the card playing were each fined 10i. and costs ; and the charges of being on licensed premises after hours were dismiße J. THE COOPER'S ARMS.

Charles Thornton, licensee of the Cooper Arms Inn, Waterloo-road, Widnes, was summoned for selling drink to a drunken man, and also for permitting drunkenness on the 25th ult., and John Murray and James Leonard were summoned for being drunk on the licensed prem- ises. Mr. Swift, who defended, said two material witnesses had been compelled to leave the court to attend the funeral of a relative, and he therefore applied for:an adjournment. The police raised no objection, and the case was adjourned to the 26th.

THE TIPPING ARMS, BOLD. James Davies, landlord of the Tipping Arms, Bold was summoned for permitting gaming on his premises on the sth inst., and Arthur Johnson, George Prescot, James Almond, and George Whitfield, were charged with aid- ing and abetting Davies in gaming.—Mr. T. Swift again defended.—P.S. Chipchase stated that about ten minutes past ten o'clock on the night of the sth inst. he was on duty near the Tipping Arms, when he heard sounds as though dominoes were being played. As he was in plain clothes he went into the house, and heard one man say "I shall win this game ; Ido not mean to pay this time." He subsequently heard the same voice say " Dominoe : I told you I should, win." He saw the men served several times with beer, and on each occa- sion money was tendered by the men who lost.—Mr. Swift contended that the defendants were not playing for money nor money's worth, and he called all the men, who corroborated that statement. The Bench after a patient hearing, said as no corroborative evidence had been given by the prosecution, the case would be dis- missed.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. PETER, CLA.RE,
div.p: DEATH OF MR. PETER, CLA.RE,

It is with much regret that we have to record the death of Mr. Peter Clare. one of the oldest tradesmen of Warrington, which took place at his residence, No. 8, Battersbv-lane, about ve o'clock yesterday morning. The deceased was seventy years of age, and tor the past 47 years has carried on business as a rope manufacturer in the neighbourhood. He was well known and highly respected, and was a mem- ber of the Wesleyan body and a strong Liberal. Some three weeks since he was attacked with in- fluerza, and being already a sufferer tram asthma he never recovered.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RLTNCOR.N, &c.
" BY IN OCCASIONAL CORIIESPONMINT."

The election in Runcorn North has been won and lost, and the defeated party have only one course, to make the best of their reverse, and prepare for another struggle when opportunity appears. Mr. Ockleston made a gallant fight, and considering the strong forces arrayed against him it is surpris- ing the majority was not more than 41. Last time Major Ilazlehurst won by over 1,000, while this time the total number of votes polled for him did not reach that number, a fact which ought to give his opponents hcpe for the future. As is quite natural there is some feeling against those Liberals who deserted their party in order to support the " Independent cry, but as they were no doubt acting conscientiously, it would be well to bury the hatchet, and let bygones be bygones.

I.must pay Major Hazlehurst the compliment of saying that he worked as though he meant to win, and on the day of election he was busier than any canvasser. His name is still a power in Runcorn, and his personal ;presence proved irresistible to the ladies who voted for him almost to a woman. I have no doubt he will endeavour to carry out his pledges in the spirit in which he gave them, and I hope that Mr.Speakman and he will be found working together on the ques- tion of reduced fares across the railway footbridge, which was powerfully advocated by Mr. Imison at one of the meetings. Sunday trains would be a boon and a blessing to the benighted Runcoruians, and the influence of the County Council might help the railway company to a speedy decision to grant Its not this boon but rig,it. The ball might be set rolling by the Commissioners sending a memorial.

Mr. W. Ockleston, the admirable, but lam sorry to say, defeated Liberal candidate for Runcorn North, for the County Council, dealing the other day with the subject of technical instruction, strongly advocated the teaching of German, and said that clerks especially wanted a knowledge of foreign languages, so that they could compete with the better educated foreigners who now came to England to usurp their places. The necessity is great indeed. In 1888 the London Chamber of Com- merce obtained statistics which showed that 35 per cent, of mercantile houses in the metropolis em- ployed foreign in preference to English clerks, "because Englishmen have no proper commercial education," and because "99 Englishmen out of 100 are acquainted with no language but their own."

It is humiliating for Englishmen to be told such things as these about themselves, but they are deplorable truths ; and Mr. Ockleston might have gone further, and pointed out the severe competi- tion from foreign workmen to which Englishmen are exposed on account of the superior education of the former. It is useless to deny such well- established facts by idle swagger about necessary British supremacy over everybody and everything foreign ; it is too late in the day for consoling our- selves in that way. It is useless also to demand as a remedy, the exclusion of foreign products and, indeed, of foreigners themselves, as some do, from the country. We must look matters squarely in the face, and set ourselves seriously to remedy them by practical means. The Board school and the technical instruction school are the best fortresses . that can be constructed as a barrier against the tide of industrial invasion, by foreigners. Hard study severe mental training, are the fighting materials there provided, and by these alone wilithe foreigner he kept from invading us in the competitive sense. Football, it has often been truly said, has helped to make our soldiers what they have been and to win our battles for us, and doubtless in case of a warlike foreign incursion, would amply prove its usefulness in making good fighting men. It is a game too that on the principle of bodily health being conducive to mental strength, plays its part in the education of the mind. But football alone, or so exclusively pursued as it is by many, will be of small service in helping us to withstand that other invasion from the continent which is so threatening our commer- cial life.

For some years Bower's Brook has been a -tand- ing bugbear to Widnes Local Board. It La; not, been a decent stream or an efficient sewer, and the money so far spent upon it has had little effect in preventing its waters flooding the gas works in time of heavy rain and placing the town in dark- ness. But it is now hoped that the brook will in future be kept within reasonable bounds and flaw unobstructed out •:,co the sea. The North Western Railway Company have agreed to enlarge their cul- verts, and the United Alkali Company have under- taken to do the remainder of the necessary work and to keep the brook cleaned out in future, which facts ore the foundation of the hope expressed above.

Some time ago the L. and N.-W. Railway Com- pany offered to give up their rights in Runcorn Ferry to Widnes Local Board if the latter would take the responsibility ot maintaining it. The Local Board have now decided to take counsel's opinion as to the liabilities of the Railway Com- pany with regard to the Ferry provided the Run- corn Improvement Commissioners will consent to pay part of the cost. I should think there will be no difficulty about this.

From what is" seen and beard" there appears every probability, although nothing definite has been communicated, that the Manchester Ship Company will construct deep docks at Runcorn in accordance with the expressed wishes of the Run- corn Board of Commissioners,and the thanks of the community are due to Mr. Lightburn, who made the subject one of the " planks " in his election address last September, and who has never missed an opportunity of pushing the matter forward since that time. That deep docks will be an immense boou to the town in fostering the trade of the port is a statement that needs no demonstration, but, if rumour speaks truly, the port is threatened with immediate danger, and the ratepayers ought to be alive to their own intereste,and avert the threatened calamity. It is said that the Ship Canal Company ore seriously contemplating closing Runcorn Docks fora period and conducting the traffic through Weston Point Docks and the Weston Canal. The reason for this course is the difficulty of reconstruct- ing tile Bridgewater Lock, which was partly de- molished by the storm a month ago, and at the same time keeping a channel open to the entrance of Runcorn Docks. In the interest of the trade and prosperity of Runcorn it is sincerely to be hoped that another way will be found out of the difficulty, and I believe other methods have been suggested. There is not the slightest doubt that the closing of the dock would drive an important part of the trade in other directions, probably to Ellesmere Port, and once gone, it would probably never return, which would be not only a loss to the town but to the Canal Com- pany as well. In the interest of all let us hops that the port of Runcorn will be kept in thorough work- ing order.

Mr. J. E. Worsley during his long connection with the coronershin for the Honour and Fee of Halton, has held many inquests on men who while under the influence of drink have met with a watery grave in he canal or docks, and he has frequently advocated that some counter attrac- tion to the public-house should be provided.in the town. He hailed with pleasure the new Seamen's Institute as likely to prove of great benefit to those who spend most of their time battling with the watery elements, and he has further shown his interest by presenting the In- stitute with an excellent bagatelle table, which bids fair to become a great source of enjoyment to the now num- erous frequenters of the place. Other amusements are also provided. Mr. and Mrs. Ebbrell and Miss 13•3wyer are doing a good work in teaching boatmen and boat women to read and write, and their efforts are much appreciated.

Mr. Whiteley the Cons,-rvative candidate for North. with Division paid a visit to Runcorn, on Wednesday by - invitation, and in the course of the afternoon was intro- duced to his principal si,spporters by Mr. J. W. Lightburn In the evenings meeting of workers was held in the small Hall of the Public Hall under the presidency of Mr. E, Imison, and he delivered an address appropriate to the occasion. Mr. Whiteley was everywhere well received and created a favourable impression. The electors generally will have an opportunity of seeing and hearing him on the 22nd inst., when a public meeting is to be held.

The annual election of members of Widnes Local Board is fixed for the first week in April, and there is some little talk that the Ratepayers Association intend to force a contest. The candidates they have chosen, I hear from a good source, are Messrs. T. Carlyle, Jas. Davies, and C. Hemingway. As the town will cer- tainly be formed into a Corporation by next November. L think the Association will be better advised and not cause about £lOO of the ratepayers' money to be spent upon a useless fight.

STEALING LEAD Faom 11111 TEMSTWOWII CO. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, Peter Fernley, labourer, of 16, Phillip-et., was charged *with stealing the previouS evening 591bs. of lead piping, value 55.. the property of the National Telephone Co., Orford-st. He was remanded till Tuesday. STEALING A WATCH.

_ At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, Alice Worrall, wife of James Wormll, of 17, Howard-st., employe(' at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s, was charged with stealing, on thepreVious Saturday, a silver watch, value £2, the property of William Briggs, pawnbroker, 18 and 20, Powys-st. It appeared from the statement of the Chief Constable and the evidence of Mr. Briggs, Miss Tunstall, and others, that the fol- lowing were the facts. The prisoner came to the prose- cutor's shop about a quarter-past ten on Saturday morning, and gat a watch, which she said was for her nephew, and agreed to pay fer it by weekly instalments. - She immediately took it to Mrs. Tunstall's, in Winwic k- at. The manageress, Miss Tunstall, was suspicious, and asked her whose the watch was, and she replied it was hers, her husband having had a pawn-ticket, and she having got it from Mr. Briggs that morning. The police were communicated with, and Detective-Sergeant Monaghan apprehended her. She denied to him the theft, and now made the same denial. She was fined 20s. and costs (£2 in all), in default a month's imprison- ment.

WIOLESALE THEFTS FROM SHOP DOORS. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, Charles Tuckwell, Wm. Munroe, Frederick Varley, and James Fritz were charged with stealing.a dozen pairs of stockings from the shop of Mr. John Sutton ; a cardigan jacket from the shop of .Mr. Tlnsworth ; and a pair of men's boots from the shop of Mr. Fleming on the 3rd inst. It appeared that the prisoners were in the habit of playing musical instruments in the street, but on the day in question they changed their occupation to "lift- ing "anything they could conveniently get bold of in front of tradesmen's shops. Their conduct excited the suspicion of the barman at the Wine Tavern, Market- street, and information was given td the police. They were all apprehended at th,,ir lodgings,where the articles mentioned were also found. Tuckwell was sent to gaol for three months,- and the other three were sent for two mouths.

A WOULD-BB BIGAMIST. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, Joseph Hankon was charged on warrant, with having on the 23rd February used malicious threats towards Eliza Clare, a domestic servant, employed at ea house in Wilson Patten-st. From a statement of the Chief Con- stable it appears that for some twelve months the defend- ant has been lodging at the mother's house, and had been "keeping company" with the complainant. He repre- sented himself as a widower, and that he had buried his wife two years ago. A short time since so,the suspicion arose as to the truth *f his statement, and Mrs. Clare communicated with the Vicar of Brymbo, at which place he had resided, previous to his coming to Warrington. The Vicar replied that Hankon was married, and that his wife and child lived there. In spite of this, defendant continued to pay attentions to the girl, and on the night ia the 20th February, he was taking her to her house. On the way he pressed her very much with a view to some arrangements being made for their marriage. She repliecithat she would do nothing. He then said, "If I don't have you, I will take both our lives."—Eliza Clare corrobnrated the Chief Constable's statement. The mother also stated that defendant used threats towards her daughter in her preEence.—lnspector Spinks deposed to arresting defendant. Ia reply to the charge, he said "I know nothing about it." He also said that his wife was dead, but the inspector told him he intended to bring the wife into court.—The wife and child of the defendant were then brought into coUrt.—The defend- ant was bound over to keep the peace for sir months, aad ordered to find a surety in the sum of £lO. rison, and Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Price was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Market-place. on Saturday evening. P. C. Wade said there was a man in the street playing an organ and with a monkey. The defendant pushed through the crowd and offered it a penny. As soon as the animal came for it he kicked it. Witness remonstrated with him, and he said he would kick it again, and was going to do so, when he appre- hended him. He was fined 10s. and costs, 178. in all. —Maurice Lynch, drunk and disorderly on Saturday night, in Bridge-street, was fined ss. and costs.—Thos. Taylor, in Market-street, on Saturday night, ss. and costs. DRUNX.—Alexander Forrester and 'James Lishman, drunk in Irlam-street, on Sunday afternoon, were fined ss. each. Tinyon, Bank Quay.— Inspector Spinks said that the man was sleeping in one of the flues leading from the furnace, a most dangerous place.—The prisoner said he had no home or work, and had only earned 7d. for the last week. The men about the works had told him there was no harm in his sleeping in the flue.—Mr. Ttnyon Said the prisoner had been warned on several Occasions not to come about the works.—The Chief-constalele said that nearly 20 years eince the pritoner was considered a very clever workman as a file cutter in the town.—lle was sent to prison for, a month's hard labour. BREACH OF THE Poem—WiTliam Connor, fish hawker, Dolman's-lane, for committing a breach of the peace in Bank-street the previous day,by assaulting John Glavin, was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for Et months. CHIMNEYS oN FIRM—Mary Ann Chesworth, Orford- street, and Thomas Coyne, labourer, Silver-square, for _haying their chimneys on fire were fined is. each. Wive ASSAULT.—RaIph Norman, a working-man, was 'charged on a warrant with assaulting his wife Margaret Norman, and was fined 20s. and costs. CHARGE OF ARMY DFSERTION.—Thoroas Bate, of Walshamoton near Ellesmere, was charged with desert- ing Her Majesty's regiment, of Seaforth Highlanders,. and was remanded for a week. TOESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and E. J. Guest. DRUNNENNESS.—Mar Garrity, was sent to gaol for 14 days, for drunkenness', and Bridget Burke, was fined ss. or seven days. A MIDNIGHT CHASE.—J. Slater, Foundry-St., was charged with being drunk on Monday night, and also with haying assaulted P.C. Cooper.—The constable stated that about 12.20 on Tuesday morning, whilst in Town's End, he heard a large number of men singing. After searching several streets he found seven men sing- ing at the top of their voices. He asked them to desist, and they did. After a little conversation several went away and left Slater and another man. As he was about to move away-, Slater suddenly struck him six blows on the mouth, drawing blood and injuring him severcly4 'The constable said that he could not protect himself, as

he was enveloped in a large cape. After committing the assault the prisoner ran away, with the constable close on his heels. The prisonei ran into the Bay Horse yard and dodged him round a cart for some time, and only left that t efuge when the constable began to blow his whistle. Leaving the yard, the prisoner rag at full speed along Hallam-lane into Win wick-at., and here he managed to elude Cooper. The constable, however, determined not to be baffled, lay in wait for the prisoner I at Foundry-st., and in a few minutes he hove in sight, but on observing Cooper,, he re-started on his career, I only to run in the arms of Inspector Spinks, who was i attracted by the uproar.—lnspector Spinks said that the prisoner, on running into his arms, implored him to pre- vent the constable from "laying him out." (Laughter.) —The prisoner said that he struck the constable in self- defence, and two witnewes were called, who stated that the constable struck the prisoner twice,without any pro- vocation.—Fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days. WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Fairclough (chair- man) and Mr. B. M. Crosfield. DRM.—Thomas Walsh, a stranger in Warrington, charged with being drunk in Bank-st., was dismissed on promising to leave the town. , WEDNESDAT.—Before Aldermad Chandley (chairman), _ . . . . .

She came from Bacup, and it bad been ascertained that she was the daughter of respectable, but poor, parents there,and left home for being remonstrated with for being late in. He was fined Be. and costs. / Plummier ENLISTMENT.—Partick Jenkins was charged with making a 'false declaration on enlistment in the South Lancashire regiment by stating that he had not been convicted of ielony. DRUNK IN CHARGE OP A HORSB.—James Broughton, tripe dresser, drunk 'in charge of a horse and cart in Mersey-et., on Thursday, was fined 10e. and costs. div.head: WARRINGTON CONFESSION OF
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CONFESSION OF
MURDER. DETAILS OF THE CRIME.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, be- fore Alderman Chandley (in the chair), and Messrs. J. Geddes, L. Voisey, and R. Garnett, Roland George Lush was brought up on remand, charged on his own confession with the murder of William Parsons, a draper, at Andover, about 30 years ago.— The Chief Constable saia he had received a com- thunication from the Hampshire police, asking for another remand for a week to enable them to con- tinue their inquiries. The prisoner could not be kept longer in the Bridewell, and Mr. Hunt asked that be might be remanded to Strangeways Jail. The prisoner was therefore remanded thither for a week.

div.head: CORONER'S JURY'S VERDICT OF WILFUL__MIIRDER.
div.p: A CORONER'S JURY'S VERDICT OF WILFUL__MIIRDER.

The "Hampshire Chronicle" gives the following par- .; ticulara concerning the crime with which the prisoner ; charges himself, which have not hitherto been published in our columns :—" The prisoner has been away from I Andover for many years. Some people consider the ! confession to be the outcome of a drunken freak, but the most general impression is that the facts are correct, and further particulars are eagerly looked for. A large ' number of the inhabitants of Andover and the neighbour- hood can vividly remember the shocking tragedy, which ' for weeks caused the utmost consternation in the dig- trict. The victim of the brutal outrage, which occurred on the night of the 21st or the early morning of the 22nd November, 1858, was a well-known tradesman named William Parsons, father of the present proprietor of the Waterloo House establishment.(Mr. William H. Parsons). A children's party was being held that evening at the residence of Mr. Parsons, and he went out with the avowed purpose of posting SOME) letters. For what pur- pose he made his way to the scene of the outrage in the Salisbury-road is a matter of conjecture. The night was very clear, and there was an intense hoar-frost. In a field abutting the Salisbury-road was a shed, and it was supposed that the victim was, on leaving this shed, followed by the assassin and murdered by means of a large-knobbed stick, which had the appearance of having been recently cut from the hedge, and was ,found lying by the side of the murdered man. The body was found in the early morning by Henry Edward Northover, an assistant at 'Mr. Parsons's establishment. The body presented a ghastly spectacle. It was lying face, down- wards, the face having been beatea into the earth, and when removed a cavity was left in the mould, being full of blood. The back of the head was battered in. Crowds had assembled in the roadway, but only those first on the scene were admitted, and the body was afterwards taken on a stretcher to the Andover Union Workhouse. An inquest was held, and following the vereict of wilful murder against some person unknown a man, Thomas Alexander Banks, the landlord of the Rose and Crown Inn, and Emma Banks, his wife, were ap- prehended Knd charged with the murder, and after several hearings they were committed for, trial at the County Assizes at Winchester. At the Assizes in the fol- lowing March the Grand Jury threw out the bill, and the prisoners were discharged." The "Andover Stan- dard" says the man Banks who was committed for trial for murder is now living at Fox Farm, and adds : " Lush is supposed to be a native of Andover, and those who were living at the time recollect a person of that name, a son of Charles Lush, at that time a coal merchant at Andover." The same paper remarks "This self-accusation is thought by some to be the out- come of a drunken freak, whilst others incline to the Idea that there is some truth in his statement, but one cannot help leaning to the former idea, when it is con- sidered that at the time of the murder, if the accused is the man he is supposed to be, he was then under 17 years of age."

div.head: SENTENCe OF DEATH.
div.p: SENTENCe OF DEATH.

James Noble, 46, chimney sweep, of Chelsea, was found guilty, at the Central Criminal Court, London,on Wednesday, of the murder of a woman named Elizabeth Swift, with whom he cohabited. The evidence went to prove that the parties had been drinking on the night of February 4th last, and on returning, to their lodginas a quarrel arose,during, which the accused cut the woman's throat. She ran to a neighbouring publie-hose, and there died. Jealousy was assigned as the motive. Mr. Justice Smith sentenced the prisoner to death.

The Rev. Dr. Lee, vicar of All Saints', Lambeth, was on Wednesday,..committed_ fin trial on the charge of misconduct with a lad named Clifton, an ex-inmate of a reformatory school. The body of a child.in an advanced state of decom- position was on Wednesday found in a chimney a t 22, Bevington-hill , Liverpool. A woman named Mary Corless is in custody. Three negroes lying in gaol at Memphis, Tennessee, on a charge of 'assaulting yoting white girls, have been lynched by.a band of seventy-five men, who broke into the building during the night. Two little children, named Rolf, were suffocated at a house in Lillington-st., Pimlico, on Thursday, by a fire which broke out during the absence of their parents. At Sheffield. on Thursday, Judge Ellison decided that the masters had a right to issue a list of workmen not to be employed by their federation. The workmen con- template appealing against the decision.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. T. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. D. Wright,B. Brown, J. Tilley, J. Taylor, S. Sadler, J. Midwood,G. I. Neil, J. Beech, T. Heyes, J. Carroll, E. Carey, H. S. Timmis, H. S. Oppeaheim (clerk), T. Craik (assistant clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), I. Carr (surveyor),, and W. Lowe (nuisance inspector).

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOT]) kLL RUGBY.

- The greatest match of the year is now a thing of tho past, and England can boast of an unbroken record. They have conquered all their international rivals and the su- premacy of English football is complete. Last season's dis- aster at Richmond has been avenged,and our countrymen are happy once more. Saturday's victory at Edinburgh was a pretty correct verification of public form, as in the previous contests against Wales and Ireland the perform- ances of the English regresentatives were a shade more satisfactory than were Wise of the representatives of the Thistle. The side that did duty for Scotland was so slightly altered from that which obtained such a signi- ficant success twelve months ago that England deserve vary great credit for beating them, and, that, too, over the Border. To win by five points to none was a great achievement, and as regards actual merit was little below the victory gained on the same ground two year! since. •

With only one change in the back division that wrought such havoc against England last season, Sect- land were supposed to have a great chance of adding t. their laurels, and yet we see how all calculations in-this direction were upset. There is a wide difference between scoring three goals and none at all, yet the backs that represented England at Richmond were generally con- sidered more formidable than those which stripped at Raeburn Place. No one outside Yorkshire had much confidence in Briggs and Varley—especially the latter,— whilst Coop's inclusion at full back was questioned in many quarters. No fault was found with the three- quarter backs, every one being admittedly really first- class, and they did not belie their reputation. Indeed,it may be stated that all the fifteen acquitted themselves admirably, and the great Scotch crowd were hearty in cheering the winning team. The combination of the English forwards might have ,been better, but the strong point about their play was their determination and energy, and it was in this department that they more than held their own.

There was little to choose between the two sets of forwards,the Englishmen doing much wore telling work than was the case last year. The Scots scrimmaged with great vigour, but , they wore not so prominent in the loose. C. E. Orr and Anderson again demonstrated their undoubted abilities at half-back, but the York- shire pair looked well after them and were by no means overaived by , their mars famous antagonists. The three-quarters were not so smart as the English three, and none could compare with Lockwood. Stevenson Once more proved a sterling full back, and it was per- haps well for England that he was not tried at centre three-quarter, where be would have been a vast im- provement on W. Neilson. 'His play was superb.

Ireland played such good football against both Eng- land and Scotland that it was not surprising to hear of their cow:pest of Wales. Their forwards were too smart for the Welshmen, whose system of four three-quarters proved ineffective against the vigorous Irishmen, with the result that Wales were sent home beaten by a goal and a try. Ireland was the stronger team throughout, and their success was immensely popular with the spec- tators who thronged the Dublin enclosure.

The ground at Park Avenue is generally so well looked after that it was disappointing to find it too hard and dan- gerous for football on Saturday. The Manchester players would only consent to an exhibition display of forty minutes' duration, so that although Bradford were vic- torious the result counts as a draw. Woods scored the only point for the visitors, who did Well up to the in- terval, but were afterwards overplayed. Doyle could not place a goal out of three chances. A reverse was in store for Salford at St. Helens, the latter winning by three tries. Some excuse can be made for the visitors lU; with Bent and others away, they were handicapped. Broughton Rangers received a terrible drubbing at Halifax. Defeat by 34 points to nil is appalling. Wakefield Trinity were equal to the best efforts of Wigant'n.ither sine being able to secure a point. Oldham Ars more fortunate against Manches- ter Rasgers, whom they vanquishSd y two goals and three tries to a try. Liverpool were too clever for Bir- kenhead Park, ai wore Rochdale Hornets for New Brighton.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

Saturday was a very buy day for followers of the Association game. Two international fixtures wete dis posed of by England, who beat both Wales and Ireland Without losing so much as a goal. These triumphs are all the more creditable as very few of the victorious players are like-1y to be given places in the great battle of the year against Scotland. . Thero is an abundance of talent to solect from this season, and if the very best men are chosen the Scotch match I ught to yield another victory.

There is apparently. lit.le to choose between west I Bromwich Albion and Notts Forest. They have met twice in the semi-tinal 'for the Football Association Cup, and a third trial will be necessary before opponents are found for Aston Villa in the final. How well the Albion and the Forest are rilalsthedis shown by the fact that in the two gatnes each has been credited with a goal, and if this is their best fain they can hardly hOpe to be suc- cessful against AstonrVilla, whichever ultimately gains an entrance to the last round'. The semi-final will have to be decided at Derby, on Wednesday afternoon next, when it must be brought to a finish somehow.

" Five League fiatures,were disposed of on Saturday, all except onescoming off prety moth as was anticipated. The exception was the contest between Burnley and the Bolton Wanderers. Seeing that the first-named had never previously lest a League match at Turf Moor there was no reason to suppose thit a' surprise was in store for them, as there is little to choose between the two teams. Dokvever, they were destined to be beaten, the Wanderers scoring .two goals to one, exactly as they did at the same place last year. North end were visited by Derby County, and although they had as much' as they could do to hold their own prior to the interval, they finally won by three goals. The North End have just secured the services of Bob Roberts, the Welsh half- back, who for the past eight years has done so much for the Bolton Wanderers. ,

There was a hard struggle between Accrington and Sunderland, but inthe end the Northerners were trium- phant. The championship seems to be a certainty for them. A good deal will depend upon the issue of the match between Sunterlaild and the North End on Satur- day next, but the former will have an advantage in being on their own ground. Aston Villa had to journey to Blackburn minus four of their best players, and were consequently leaten, although they were in front at the conclusion of the first half. Stoke were also ' short- handed at Everton as their goalkeeper and full backs were assisting England at Belfast, Despite this draw- back, however, they only lost by a, goal,. after having quite as much of the play as their antagonists. The win was much appreciated by the Liverpool team, who have had their share of vicissitudes latterly. The rival factions in the'ctubare stitl continuing their hostility to- wards each other. ' "

Lady Egidia Hastings, the only daughter, of Lord POnington, died on Monday night at Pau. She was only 22. ' It has been agreed that Daisy Hopkins's action against Rev. F. Wallis shall be held at Ipswich on or about the 23rd inst. Those slaughterhouse level railway crossings An un- known woman has been cut to pieces on one of them at Lower Edmonton. An Oriental who is alleged to have scandalised the people of Suresnes, near Paris, by keeping a harem, has been evicted from the house. The 'Steamship Eider was on Monday lifted from the Blue Slipper Itock at Atherley, Isle of Wight. It is in- tended early next week to make the attempt to tow her off.

The Clerk said he had received a leiter from the East- bourne Corporation soliciting the assistance of the Local Board in opposing the Bill promoted by the Salvation Army with regard to the Eastbourne Local Act.—The communication was laid on the table on the motion of the Chairman.

div.head: TDB MINHRS' STRIKE AND OAS.
div.p: TDB MINHRS' STRIKE AND OAS.

The Gas and Water Committee reported that the gas had been twice tested during the month and was found to be 17.64 and 16.34 candles, respectively; free from sulphuretted hydrogen. The shooting right of Fex Hill had been leased to Mr. Bretherton for a term of 5 years, at a rental of a per annum. The engineer reported that, ' in view of the projected stoppage of all collieries on the 12m prox. the stocks of coals both at the Pumping Stations and the Gas Works have, during the last 10 days, been increased as much as possible. Extra supplies have been bought from the Gas Works, and, if the coal is delivered as at present arranged for, the stock by the 12th prox. will be 1500 tons or equal to five weeks' supply. The Rainfall for the month has been :—A mean 2.045 inches. Water in stock Feb. 24, 1892-8,247,412 gallons. Mr. Brown in moving the adoption of the minutes referred to the strike of miners, and said the coal was coining in very well, and the Committee now felt safe for five weeks' supply of gas to the township.— Passed.

div.head: IMPORTANT HIGHWAY DEPROTHRIIRTB.
div.p: IMPORTANT HIGHWAY DEPROTHRIIRTB.

The Highway Conimittee reported that the surveyor submitted plans and estimate for the sewering and im- provement of Lowerhouse-land in accordance with the directions of the Board. Recommended that such plans and estimate be approved, and that, subject to the com- pletion of the agreement with the trustees of the Leigh Estate, application be made to the Local Government Board for its sanction to the borrowing of £5,64.0, the amount estimated to be required to execute the works. Milton-road—Recommended that,subject to the arrange- wienti4 with respect to the improvement in Lowerhouse- lane referred to in the last previous recommendation being completed, the Surveyor's plans and estimate now submitted for sewering Milton-road from a point oppo- site the house premises, No. 25, Milton-road, to Lower- house-lane, and thereto form . a junction with the new sewer proposed to be constructed in Lowerhouse-lane, ofc also approved; and that application be made to the Local Government Board at the same time as the appli- cation with regard te Lowerhouse-lane„ for the sanction to the borrowing of the amount estimated to be required to carry out the works, viz. £360. Mr. Sadler moved and Mr: Taylor seconded the adop- tion of the minutas.—Mr. Tilley suggested that that the Board should carry out the improvements in Lower House-lane themselves, and so find employment for those who were now on the streets out of work.
directi,
ROAD MHXDING.

Mr. Heys drew attention to she extraordinary way in which the roads in the upper portion of the township were beingrepaired, if it could be called repaired. Material varying in size from a turnip to the size of the surveyor's head was being placed upon the roads and leftlupon them uncovered and unrolled, ad in con- sequence there was great danger to vehicles. Other roads Were repaired in sueh an artistic fashion that they were .as bad as ever in the course of a few weeks.—Mr. Beech supported Mr. Tilley's suggestion.—Mr. Midwood pointed out that the original estimate for Lowerhouse- lane was something over £4,000, and now it had risen to £6,ooG.—Mr.Sadler in reply to Mr. Tilley said his sug- gestion would be considered at the proper time, but the contracts were not yet in. In answer to Mr. Miawood, he pointed out that sewering and road-snaking was not included in the rough estimate, it was found advisable to carry out, and at the wise ifuggestien of Mr. Taylor the size of the pipes had been increased. ' They had also to provide compensation to a considerable extent. Than the road from Steward's-lane to Birchileld-road, which would be taken over by the County C•uncib as a main road, required an outlay of £468 before that could bake place.

div.head: LI7GSDALN BRIDGE.
div.p: LI7GSDALN BRIDGE.

Mr. Tilley said the surveyor reported that ,the brick- work of Lugsdale Bridge had suffered from the severe frost and floods, and would require re-painting, and he (Mr. Tiller) remarked that he supposed it was through bad building that the bridge was giving way. It ,was never intended to be built where it was, and it was, besides, in the wrong form. It could have been made straight wherever it was crooked. He contended that the culvert could have been ,carried straight through at a cost of £l5O, but it had cost £5OO and £6oo.—Mr. Sadler said the bridge had been built in accordance with the specifications and plans that were placed before the Board and approved of without opposition. It was now too late to raise an objection.
HEALTH ODIHMITTiE,-SULPHURETTED.HYDROGHT

The -Seaitt;Committee's minutes contained a repOrt by the Glerk, who said he had had an interview with the secretary of the United Alkali Company with respect to the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen in the district, and the secretary had stitszd that the Company were doing all in their power to minimise any nuisance afising from their works, and had appointed inspectors whose duty it was to watch the works night and day in order to detect any irregularity, and, at ,the present time, they con- tended, no appreciable nuisance emanated from their works.—The Medical Officer (Dr. O'Keeffe) reported that during February there had been 98 births anti 50 deaths, being at the respective rates of 39.2 and 1935. per 1.000. Sixteen cases of infectious diseases had been notified. Complaints had been made to hitp by residents in Hutchinson-At. of being injuriously affected in health by the inhalation of sulphuretted hydrogen gas. At that time the wind was from a westerly direction. —Mr. Wright moved, and Mr. Tilley seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Beech said he had auout 2t notices from the Nuisa,nce Inspector calling upon him to re-construct or rebuild closetS, andthe said on visiting those places three-fourths of them were in such a condition that neither the Inspector nor himself could possibly tell what they required, because they wanted emptying and cleansing. There seemed to be a great deal of time wasted in visiting the property owners, who were put to a great deal of unnecess iry inconveni- ence. Mr. Wright said the Committee did not always get the help from the property owners with respect to, closets that they were entitled te). With respect to the manner in which the work was done, it certainly never was Oone so well as it was done by the Board's own officials (Mr. Buck : Queition—The minutes were passed.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary meeting of this Board was held at the Dutton Union, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Mr. Mclntyre (chairman), the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Dr. Steel, and Messrs. J. Knowles, J. Stokes, J. Whitlow, T. Baxter, C.C., J. Edwards, U. E. Heywood, T. Lewis, J. Baguley, J. Brandreth,, P. Hall, E. Bretherton, J. Hall, W. Pickering, T. Lea, J. W. Lightburn, P. Speakman, S. Taylor, W. Turner, E. Aaron, Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and Mr. Dansey, Local Government Board inspector. RESIGNATION OF DR. WEATER.

The Clerk read a letter from' Dr. Weaver, Medica, Officer and Public Vaccinator for Prodsnam, resigning his appointment on account of his leaving the district. He had, he said, held the offices for 29 years, and in sur- rendering his trust he begged to thank the Board for the courtesy and friendship he had always experienced from it during that long period.—Mr. Heywood proposed that the resignation be accepted, and that the Clerk be in- structed to write to Dr. Weaver conveying the best wishes of the Board for his future happiness.—Mr. Baxter seconded, and the motion was carried.—The Clerk was instructed to advertise for a successor to Dr. Weaver, at the same salary, LBO a year.
, THE -ELECTION. On the proposition of Mr. Brandreth, it was resolved that the Clerk be allowed £2O, expenses as returning officer in the forthcoming election of Quardians.

THE PROVISION OF TRAMP WARDS. Mr. Dansey consulted the Board as to plans for new tramp wards sent in February to the Local Government Board as revised plans,but said they were the same plans as had been submitted to them in November. It was decided in February, he reminded the Board, to have two alternative plans—for a room in which a numuer of tramps could be accommodated together, and for separ- ate cells. Be had understood that the plans for the cells were to be altered to Provide for these be- ing wider, but the plans had not been altered. The Workhouse Master said, in consequence of the Ship Canal being so far adv4anced towards completion, the number of vagrants had very much decreased, and he thought this acconimddation for them would not be necessary. Some conversation took place as to the re lative advantages of having an " associated ward " and separate cells.—Mr. Dansey expressed himself in favour of the former. The law, he said, as to vagrants might be Altered, and separate cells could not be used for any other purpose. but a room Could be.—Mr. Aaron strongly ob- jected to the associated ward. He said it would be dan- gerous to have a number of able-bodied tramps together instead of isolated, in that House, which was not sur- rounded by police like town workhouses, and in which most of the mates were cripples. If an outbreak occur- red among them they might be unmanageable, and might set fire to the place.—Mr. Dansey did not think there would be any danger from the adoption of the associated ward.—Mr. Heywood said there was no doubt the canal was finished temporarily, but it was about to start again, and the tramp wards might be wanted before long. As the Board bad gone to the ex- pense of having plans they ought to have them correct. —On the motion of Mr. Speakman, seconded ba, Mr. Taylor, they were referred back to the Building Com- mittee ; the suggestions of Mr. Dansey to be communi- cated to the architect. _
There was no other business of consequence.
