"„• Sacral:sirlee of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten . .
on'Wedneliday morning. - RUGBY. WARRLNGTON v. MOSSLEY. Visitors to Wilderspool on Saturday were fully prepar-

ed for Seeing the locals pile on an immense score against the Mossleyites, for the recollection of Warrington haying inflicted a three goals and a try beating on the first engage- ment warranted such an assumption. Although the

game WaS of a one-sided nature, it was nevertheless interesting throughout, and one point noticeable in the afternoon's sport was the good flan% which prevailed. In favourable weather, and befoie an average " gate,"
Turner kicked off towards the pavilion goal, and

England's return being misjudged by Heesom, the first few items occurred in midfield. Buckley came through a pack, and dribbled into Mossley quarters, and play was rendered a trifle monotonous until Mossley, with an extra spurt, Eagland being the leading operator, changed be venue to the Warrington lines. The unexpected bold front presented by the visitors was encouraged to a high degree by the onlookers, but Warrington, who had been lagging in their combination, now buckl d to, and a free kick taken by Turner was succeeded by James and John Bate passing, the former clearing beautifully, and pass- ing to Jolley, who was promptly collared. Webster received in close quarters, and made no headway, but James Bate next dodged over, but, fortunately, lost possession. Evans, Ashton, John Bate, and Berry aided the Warringtonians to maintain the pressure, and Morrell temporarily cleared. Turner soon had the oval on the Mossley lines once more, and then a sequence of passing by Evans, the Bates, Heesom, and Webster was followed by some brilliant exchanges, Taylor's kick ending in Webster making his mark at his quarter flag. John Bate passed out to Heesom, but Eagland tackled him well, whilst the compliment was returned a moment later, when Radley transferred to Eagland. Lawton kicked well, and the oval was sent dead. Berry and James Bate passing well, some strong rushes headed by Teare and Knowles, placed the home side in the ascendency again, but Tayler promptly replied and Mossley pressed. The attack was brief, but James Bate throwing to Evans, the latter punted to Morrell, who failed to field the oval, and Randles passing to Evans, the latter got over with Morrell clinging to his shoulders. The point was promptly negatived, but from this point the chances of Mossley were indeed forlorn. The com- bination of Wayington irnprbved at every stage, and although the visitors reached the half-way flag on one occasion, it ended in disaster for them. A scrimmage near the centre line saw the Bates and Fleesorn passing in their unique style, and although Webster failed at the first' attempt to take the centre's pass, he dribbled up to Morrell, and a fast follow-up saw the visiting custodian safely held. The movement was respon- sible for James Bate scoring from the pack which fol- lowed;and the easy place was converted by Heesom. Buckley and Jolley were prominent on the drop-out, and a series of scrimmages being stoutly contested on the line, the monotony was relieved when Heesom with ft tricky bit of play nearly brought about the downfall' of the Mossley goal. Evans failed at a pass from Ran- dies by the merest shade, and although Taylor cleared, Heesom's effective tackling did not allow of much pro- gress. Buckley got clear on one occasion in fine- style' but finally passed to Eagland, and danger Was averted, and although Heesorri was a shade slow from a pass by John Bate, success awaited Warrington the .next 'min- ute, for the oval was found to be careering near the Mossley line, and Thorniley picking, up in the loose, passed to Evans, who ran in near the corner. Turner's finely-placed goal from touch was applauded to the echo. With two goals of a lead ends were changed, and the second half was of a =Pre one-sided nature than its predecessor. A fine rush by the Mossleyites direct from the restart saw the Warrington line in danger, but a beautiful sequence of passes by James and John Bate and Heesom was aided by Thorniley heading the for- wards well into Mossley territory. Some loose play followed, and Evans, nipping up the oval, dodged through, and scored in a position to enable him to augment. Radley had a fine chance for Mossley soon after the restart, but preferred to pass, and after a long spell at half way, Ashton and Jolley' led pp tip the attack being maintained. James Bate tricked beautifully, and Turner made an effort, but being held near the linete handed over to Jolley, who was placed in a like predi- cament, and Randle.; woe the lucky party to complete the effort. Evans this time failed at goal. Mossley now want from bad to worse, and after Teare and Heesom had forced the game on their lines, John Bate get finely away from a scrimmage, and, passing to Bee- son), the latter completed one of the most finished tries of the day. Turner failing to augment. A mistake by ' Morrell allowed Buckley to score in an easy position directly on the restart, and with Ideesom kicking a goal, the final result read—Warrington, 4-2-2 ; Moseley, Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back ; H. Webster, F. Heesom, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs ; James Bate, and John Bate, half-backs ; H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Randles, H. Teare, Buckley, J. T. Thorniley, J. Knowles, and J. J3erry, forwards. Mossley : Merrell, back : Taylor, Eaglalad, and W. Law- ton, three-quarter back) ; *James Lawton and Radley, half backs • Walker, Newby, Cunningham, Corscadden, Lawton, Iblfs, Marshall, Marland, and Radley, forwards. WARRINGTON "A" Y. OLD EDWAEDIANS "A."—Al- though rather cold, the weather was all that could he desired when this match took place on the Warwick- shire County Cricket ground. The home team started the game. The ball was quickly rushed back, and a bout of fine passing by the visiting backs soon saw the leather careering around the home. lines. While the game was waging in the Old Edwardians' quarter a splendid bit of passing by Antrobus and Lally gave Daniels possession, and, dodging a couple of opponents, be dropped a very pretty goal. A complete change fol.' lowed, the smartness of the Warrington players being applauded, and Flampson, Molyneux, Bailee, and Westall dribbling over, the last-named scored. 'No sooner had the ball been re-started than Forster, Warburton, and Hampscn headed a loose dribble, and Lally, picking op, threw to Antrobus, who handed on to Daniels for the iatter to score, and Sampson placed a goal. Warrington stilt continued to pepper away at the oppesing goal, Potts almost dashing over, but up to half-time nothing further was scored. lee-starting, the game was at once taken into the home quarters. Davies made a strong run to the line. Dropping out, the leather wlas returned by Sampson, and Hanipson pouncing on the ball made a fine dribble, Westall completing •the try. The Old Ed- vrardians could make no head against the fine passing exhinited by their opponents, until a kick eventually sent the oval into the visitors' half. It was qnickly re- turned, and some clever work ended' in the ball being passed out to Potts, who ran in at the corner flag. Davies next made a strong rush, and the ball being passed to Ashurst, this player scored under the posts. Warrington still continued to have .all the best of the play against their big antagonists, Westall gaining another try, and W. Warburton two tries, the final score reading—Warrington 4-5-2 to 0-0-1. Si. HELENS V. SALFORD.—ThiS fixture Was played at St. Helens on Saturday afternoon, before 3,000 specta- tors. The St. Helens men played down hill in the first half, and from the start had the upper hand. Cross put in some grand work, and a timely pass by him to Ren- nie enabled the latter to score a splendid try near the corner flag, five minutes from the commencement. The visitors afterwards tried hard to secure an equalising point, but half time was called with St. Helens leading by one try to nil. ' On the change of ends play became. very fast and exciting. The homesters were again the first to put on pressure, and Dale notched another try. Cross made a grand run tip the centre, and the ball watt transferred to Ronnie,sho again scored, and St. Helens wort a good game by three tries ksix points) to nil, , Sr. HELENS RECREATION V. LANCASTER "A" TEAMS. —This match was played at St. Flelens. on Saturday last. The Recs, were the winners by I try 11. minors, to Lan- caster 8 minors. ST. HELENS RECREATION V. LANCASTER.—On Saturday the Recs. played the return match at Lancaster, in the presence of about 3,000 spectators. Unfortunately, the Recs. were considerably weakened by the absence of several prominent members of the team, including Turton, Peter and Ralph Fildes, and Winstanley, and were actually two men short, while the homesters had mustered their full strength. The result was Lancaster 1 goal, 5 tries, and 6 minors; Recreation 1 try and 5 minors. Rl:won/4 v. Om Bora '(Livetteon).—Playet at Run- corn, on Saturday, before a large number of spectators. The visitors were short of several good men and suf- fered defeat to the extent of 2 goals, 3 tries, and 5 minors to nothing. Davies scored-4 tries and Abrams one.

div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOC-lIT-I-0.-.N—R-B-9.11RV-E v. WIDNES PARISH I Claims RESERVE.—The return fixture of these teams was played on Saturday, at Widnes. The visitors went with a poor team, but made a good show against the horn il team. Widnes kicked off, and at once pressed, but Mather and Lavall soon relieved with a grand dribblo to the visitors' goal, and Newton had hard lines in not scoring. For some time the home team again pressed, only to find Dutton as safe as ever at back. During a portion of the game the visitors had matters their own way, but could not score, half-time arriving with nothing scored. On the resumption'of Dlav, Jones in goal had plenty to do, he playing a splendid game 1 throughout. After a bit of scrambling play under the visitors' goal, the home team managed to put one through, which won them the game. Final score Parish Church, one goal ; Warrington Reserve, none. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. PENKETH.—This return fixture came off on the ground of the latter. There had been some misarrangement regarding the fixtures, two teams having turned up to play Penketh, viz., Widnes parish Church, and Warrington. The home team very pluckily decided to meet the two teams. Widnes trying conclusions with them first, time being shortened to 25 minutes each way. Penketh scored one goal iu the first

half, while Widnes were unable to equalize. The second portion of the game was very even, neither side being able to score. The game ended in favour of Penketh by one goal to Widnes none. The Penketh team played Warrington, they arranging to play half an hour each way. The home team had the benefit of the opening ex- changes, Penketh going off with a dash, but Davies re- lieved, and the half-backs transferred play to Penketh end, the visitors keeping up a continual fusillade,but the home goal-keeper and backs played a stern defence, Lewis being noticeable. At last, from pass by Nor- man, Pierpoint scored a " beauty " for Warrington, half- time arriving shortly' afterwards, with the score un- altered. Restarting, some give-and-take play ensued for a time, but Warrington soon settled down to work; but k try as they would they could not force any addition to their score. At last, however, Ball took advantage of an opening, and scored an easy goal, Warrington thus winning a poor game by 2 goals to Penketh nothing.

div.head: CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED. SUICIDE AT
div.p: CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED. SUICIDE AT

WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before Aldermen Oreenall (the Mayor), Harrison and .Wright, Timothy Sauce, tailor, of Corporation Buildings, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Corporation-st., on Sunday morning, and James Sauce, his sou, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by cutting his throat also with threatening to cut his mother's throat the same night.—Police Sergeant Smith de- posed to going to the house of the defendants with Inspector Spinks in consequence of complaints about them and finding Timothy behaving in a very violent and abusive way. As they came out at the front door Timothy came running after them with a yard brush threatening to do for Inspector Spinks. They took him in custody, and he became very rough, but with the help of P.C. Marsh thoy got him to the police station.—The defendant said the ' reason the charge wh.4 made was that he said to Inspector Spinks" You are a great man since you have been carrying a stick."-Mrs. Sauce gave evi- dence against the prisoner James Sauce, and in a r very rambling and inzoherent statement, told the 1 magistrates that he had cut his throat with a razor and threatened to cut hers also with it.—The defen- dant pleaded not guilzy to the charge.—Catherine Sauce, his sister, corroborated her mother, and said he threw an ashpan at her.—lnspector Spinks said after locking up Timothy Sauce, he went back with Sergeant Smith to the defendant's house and James's mother said she dare not stop in the house as he had threatened to Out her throat, and had cut his own. He hd a clear cut on the right . side of his neck, and it was bleeding. Witness said " Whatevet have you been doing ?" and the pris- oner replied" I don't know: I have had a drop of drink." lie was not Sober, and he was locked up. —Timothy Sauce, took his eon's part and said hie mother and sister did not know what they were saying, and they wanted to transport the poor fel- low. Anybody could see that the cut he had was not from a razor. It showed,no love on their part

to bring him to that court-house on such charges.— Inspector Spinlt's said Timothy was a decent fellow on the whole, but he'would stick up for. his ion; he had been to the station two. oethree timesltbout was fined b's. and James was bound over in the shm of £5 to keep the peace for six months; in default 14 days.

DUTTON UNION RURAL -81NITA.RY AUTHORITY. The ordinary meeting of this Authority was held at the Dutton Union, on Tuesday afternoon. 'There were present Mr. J. Mclntyre (chairman), the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs, J. Baguley,J. Edwards, Aaron, J. Knowles, J. Stokes, J. Whitlow,T. Baxter, C. C., H. E. Heywood, T. Lewis, J. Brandretli, P. Hall, E, Bretherton, J. Hall, W. Pickering, W, Tur- ner, Ashton (clerk), and Farrington (nuisance in- spector).
DRAINAGE ON .711 E. AS4TOE ESTATE.

The Clerk said the Adthority would. rernember that some nionths ago notice was saved upon the owners of the Ashton Estate and the Railway Company to sup- ply water to some cottages on the estate. He read a reply he had receivedfrom the Local Government Board to a letter of his concerning the matter. The Local Government Board forwarded a copy they had received from Mr: C. E. Linaker, Land Agency and -Estate Officers, Frodsham, on the suuject. In this he stated' that he had had a5O feet 2 inch boring put down on the site suggested by-Mr. Farrington, the Sanitary Inspec- tor, as being the most likely, on which a good supply of water couldr be obtained. The result of the boring was very unsatisfactory„ there not being a ,drop of water to be met with during the whole 'course." He , enclosed a copy of a letter received from Messrs. Tim- - mine, who he-said had had very large experience in boring for water, aud were strongly of opinion that 1 there was no chance of finding any at anything like-a reasonabln depth. LAND FOR A PUMPING STATION. The Clerk produced the provisional agreement for the purchase of land for a pumping station at the Water- works at Frodsharn land the Authority's seal was affixed thereto. . POLLUTION OF THE WESTON CANAL- . _

The Clerk read a report of a.me3ing at Weston,of the committee 'appointed to . consider, the question. of the alleged 'passing of sewage into the ,Weston 'canal! from. Sandy-lane. of which complaint hadteen made, by Mr., Collier. The cemtnittee had inspected the sewerand the houses that drained into it. The Clerk reported. that ,he bad since ascertained that prior to the :construction, of the Runcorn and Weston canal thereWetnthree cottages and a stable Which drained into the Sewer, then an open ditch, and that the outfall of this was cut off by the construction of the callal. 'He 'had also ascertained that by the Runcorn and Westoirdanal Act, 185 section 5; the Earl of Ellesmere was -empowered to make the canal, , and, amongst other thingsoto,divert or alter either tem- porarily, orpermanently the enurse of any brook, stream, or watercourse, provided he did as little -.damage as pos- sible, an full satisfaction to all persons suffering damage. The canal was now vested with the Man- chester Ship Canal Co., subject to the provisions in the Act of ISS. • If, therefOrk the Ship Canal Co.. insisted upon the sewage from Sandy-lane being Prevented from going into the canal they roust provtde another. outfalL He had referred to an agreement dated November 9th, 1886, between the Bridgewater NavigatiOn Co. and the Mersey Salt and Brine co and the Sanitary, Authority,: but could got rind that this in any way relieved the Ship Canal Co.' from providing a fresh &Alan for the sewer. The Clerk was directed to try to find thei plans of the drainage of the distriot, which were not discoverable at present, so as tObe able to refer to them in such eases in future ;and to keep. an index of all, plans in his custody. He was also instructed to write to Ili. Collier informing him that the Akuthority themselves consideradtiin not liable in the matter complained of.,

rum MEDICAL OFFICER. • On the motion of Mr. Edwards, BY. Adams was re-ap- pointed Medical Officer to the Authority., at the smile salary, £l2O, a year; and he thanked the 13oard. Via cumit's Wants On the proposition of Mr. Brandreth, seconded by Mr. Aaron, it was resolved that the Clerk's salary be £B5 per annum, A COmmlttee waS appointed to consider as to tha amount that should be allowed him for legal extras. DEFAULTING TO'ArNSICIPS. It was reported that several townships had not paid their calls, and the Clerk was directed to give notice ' that they must pay within seven days, or steps would , be taken to compel payment. There was no other boainess of importance.

DR. HOUSTON AND THE HALF-HOLIDAY
MOVEMENT.

Sir,—Kindly insert in your next issue of your valu able paper, the enclosed letter which I have received from Dr. Houston re Half-Holiday Movement.—l am, dear sir, yours truly, S. N. GREEN. 117, Liverpool-road, March 11th, 1892. [copy.] (On Circuit.) Omagh, co. Tyrone, March 10, 1892.

Dear Mr. Green,—As already wired, your invitation to the meeting convened by the Warrington Shop Assis- tants' Association, in support of the Half-Holiday Move- ment, only reached me here to-day. lam very sorry that the meeting happened to be held at a time when in any case I could not possibly attend, owing to profes- sional engagements on circuit. I trust, however, that my telegram made it clear that I was in sympathy with the movement. lam quite sure that the proposed con- cessions can he yielded without loss to shopkeepers or inconvenience to the customer. Experience shows that the public quickly and easily fall in with any reasonable adjustment of shop hours ; and there seems to me to be an actual gain all round by the reduction of those hours to the lowest limit consistent with the efficient transaction of business. On the one hand, the waste of time caused by the assistant having wearily to wait, doing nothing, for the arrival of customers who, if the closing hour were earlier, would have come earlier to buy, is avoided. On the other hand, the shopkeeper himself obtains by the shortening of business hours an accession of much needed leisure, while in the matter of lighting, heating and other expenses, there must be an economy which, taken in the aggregate, is of a substantial amount. Of course it is necessary that the movement should be sufficiently general to prevent the shopkeepers who fall in with it, from being losers by the diversion of the trade (that would otherwise go to them) to those who refuse to join the movement. lam certain, however, that the shopkeepers of Warrington will meet your Asscciation in so friendly and generous a spirit, and with such practical unanimity, that your efforts will be crowned with success.—Believe me, yours faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON.

div.head: LYIIII.
div.p: LYIIII.
BALL.—On Tuesday evening, a social ball was held at the Conservative Club, and was well attended. Dancing commenced at eight, and was continued until an early hour the next morning. -- -

LECTUIIE ON FRUIT CULTURE—On Tuesday evening a lecture en fruit culture was delivered in the Grammar School. There was a good attendance of cottagers, and the lecture, which was of an interesting character, was attentively listened to. LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—The election notices are now out, signed by the returning officer. The last day for nominations is 23rd March. Votirg papers will be distributed on the 28th March, collected on the Ist April, and counted on the 2nd. WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE MEETINO.-A meeting of the Band of Hope in connection with the Wesleyan -Chapel was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. Mr. F. 0. Moston was in the chair. Mr. John Young, of Sand- bach, delivered an interesting address. Recitations, dialogues, &c., were creditably rendered by the children, after which Mr. Brig gave a reading, entitled "The Razor Seller."

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PENN-AM AsSOBTATION FOOTBALL CLl7ll.—On Saturday evening, in connection with the Penketh Association Football Club, a supper and social even- ing was held in the Conservative Club, Stocks-lane. There was a large attendance, over 100 sitting down to tea, which was an excellent one, and much ap- preciated. The tea was prepared and the tables presided over by the following ladies :—Mrs. J. Routledge, jun., lilisses L. Routledge, Hobson, Shaw Lucy Davies, and Maggie Wilkinson. After tea the room was re-arranged, and an excellent programme, consisting of songs, &c., was gone through. Mr. J. Lewis (captain) opened the proceedings with a short and appropriate speech, which was much applauded. The musical entertainment which fol- lowed, was a very agreeable one, and was taken part in by the following gentlemen, viz. :—Messrs. Spensley, Leo, Forster, A. Appleton, A. Golding, Bal- mer, A. Greenhalgh, T. Erns, M. Woodward, and Winstanley. Messrs. C. Davies,' E. Foster, and J. Davies accompanied on the pianoforte. At the end of the programme a pleasant evening was brought to a conclusion by the singing of the National An- them. The whole of the arrangements were carried out by Mr. R. Routledge, the club secretary.

THE EXAMLNER, SATURDAY, MARCH 12 1892. BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. I SHOP ASSISTANTS' HALF- (MIXED.) HOLIDAY. MOVEMENT IN WARBINOTON. PUBLIC MEETING. On Thursday evening a largely attended public meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- st., Warrington, in aid of the movement for a weekly half-holiday for shop assistants. Mr. T. Morris pre- sided, and amongst others present were the Rector of Warrington (Rev. F. IV. Willis), Rev. .1. Gunnell, Councillors H. Roberts, .1. Shaw-Gieen, T. Flood, J. Hill ; Messrs. J. S. Garland, J. Walker, W. Roberts, F. Loughlin, S. Kenyon, &c. Mr. S. N. GREEN, the treasurer of the movement, read communications which had been received from several gentlemen. He had, he said, received a tele- gram from Dr. Houston which stated that the re- quest to attend the meeting had reached him while upon circuit in Tyrone. He regretted not being able to be present, but the movement had his hearty approval. (Loud applause.) He should gladly have spoken, if permitted, in its support, and he wished their efforts complete success. Mr. W. P. Skelton wrote that the object of the meeting had his deepest sympathy and support. He knew from practical experience that no body of workers were more en- titled to a half-holiday than were shop assistants. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. E. Brassey, high sheriff of Cheshire, wrote approving of the meeting, and the Rev. J. Warnock, in a letter, stated that he heartily sympathised with the shopassistants in their half-holiday movement. The Secretary of the Chester Shop Assistants' Association wrote that out of 445 trades- men in Chester 400 of them were closing, and he re- marked that many of the 45 who declined to close were men in so good a position that they could retire from business altogether if they wished, yet poorer tradesmen were closing their shops for the benefit of the whole. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. J. Yonge, in a letter, stated that he was unable to leave the house owing to illness, but he expressed the hope that the shop assistants would be successful in their efforts for a weekly half-holiday. (Applause.)—Dr. Gornall and Messrs. Eustauce, jewellers also wrote expressing their sympathy with the move- ment. —Alderman Francoinb wrote that, much as he would like to see the shop assistants get their half-holiday, still he was afraid that Warrington was not yet ripe for such a change. He asked if early closing would not answer the wishes of the assistants? (Dissent and some applause.) If so, then he thought the good sense of the shopkeepers would prompt them to give those in their employ an occasional half-holiday. ("Oh," and laughter.) At the present time the shopkeepers of Warrington had to contend with very severe competition from Liverpoo and Manchester, and he was afraid that a recognised half-holiday would tend to make competition more severe —Mr. Green added that Mr. T. Lowery, of Liverpool, who had been expected, was not able to attend owing to another engagement. The Dullness?, who was received with applause, expressed himself as earnestly in favour of that move- ment. What they had to do was, for the most part, to induce the middle-class people of the town, not to do their shopping on a Thursday afternoon. (Hear, hear.) His wife, for one, said she would not spend a penny in a shop if they kept open on a Thursday afternoon, and she- said there were a good many ladies of the same mind as herself. (Loud applause.) He might tell the shop keepers of Warring on that they would not lose by closing their shops on a Thursday. (Hear, hear.) If well-to-do people went to Liverpool or Manchester to make purchases, they went on other days besides Thurs- day, and they generally went on fine days, as they thought that by making purchases there they would save their train fare and thus have a cheap holiday. (Hear hear.) That money, would not, in any case, go Into the pockets of the shopkeepers of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the workinemen's half-holi- day on the Saturday, he said he did not believe that the employers of those men had been one penny the worse off for the half-holiday. He was told that 90 per cent. of the shopkeepers of Warrington were in favour of the half-holiday. If the other 10 percent. could not be won, well let them be boycotted. (Applause and laughter.) He did not like the word, but unless they could give him some tangible reason for not having mercy upon the shop assistant they deserved 'boycotting. (Loud applause.) The Recroa, who was warmly received, said there were two great reasons in favour of that movement. The first was the health of the young, both men and women. (Hear, hear.) He believed it was absolutely necessary that the young should have a half-holiday in the week. He was much more in favour of a half-holi- day than of shortening the hours—(applause)—because he did not see how the assistants were to be able to indulge in any recreations unlessthey had a half-holiday. (Hear, hear.) The other reason was that the young should have enjoyment so that their life might be as bright and happy as possible. (Applause.) There were difficulties in the way, and they must not ignore those difficulties. He knew that these were days of keen com- petition, but just as he thought all the publiciaus would be willing to close their houses on a Sunday if their neighbours would all close, so he sup- posed tradesmen would he quite willing to close their shops if all other tradesmen would do the same. It would be a great honour to Warrington if they could set an example to Liverpool and Manchester in that respect. (Hear, hear.) He should wish to see the movement carried one step farther,so that the hours might be shortened on Saturday evenings. (Loud ap- plause.) He did not see how any man could properly observe the Lord's Day if he was to be at work till a very late hour on Saturday nights. He was anxious, there- fore, that they should both have their half-holiday on the Thursday and shorter hours on the Saturday. (Loud applause.) Mr. J. S. GARLAND moved "That this meeting is strongly in favour of the efforts of the shop assistants of this town to procure a weekly half-holiday, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to bring their efforts to a successful issue." He was glad to see Mr. Morris in the chair that evening, and to see the Rector of War- rington and other ministers were lending their ,coun- tenances to that movement. He was also glad to see members of the Warrington Corporation there. He did not know whether they had any members of the Markets Committee there—(a voice :"One")—but if there were he should be very glad if they would use their influence with a view to taking the first step with regard to the early closing of the markets on Sat urday night. (Hear hear and applause). If the markets were closed at 10 o'clock on Saturday nights, he thought they might prevail upon other tradesmen to close their shops at nine o'clock. If they could make nine o'clock the latest hour for closing shops on the Saturday night that would, he thought, be a very great advantage to their young men. (Hear hear). That movement had been adopted in most other towns throughout the United Kingdom. For his own part he did not see why their assistants should be worse off than hank clerks, solicitor's clerks, and people of that class, who had the half-day on the Saturday as well as the shorter hours throughout the week. He did not think that, with all the competition they had, if they adopted the half-holiday they would be any the worse off at the end of 12 months than they were now. (Hear hear and loud applause). Mr. T. S. KENT, in seconding the proposal, said they had gone in for a half-holiday and they meant to have it. Some people said their fathers worked many more hoers than they did, and one gentlemen told him that they had too many holidays already. But he could not tell him when the holidays came in (Hear hear and laughter.) He contended also that the mental strain in all branches of business was greater to-day than in the days of their fathers. Some might say that shop assistants did not feel that, but he should just ask those who said 'hat to get some of the customers they had to serve. (Hear, bear and laughter.) He did not think employers would lose by the change, while the assistants would be able to throw much more heart into their work if they had the half-holiday once a week. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr, JOHN WALKER, in supporting the resolution, said he thought the way out in that movement was to first get the half holiday, and then, following upon that, to equalise the hours, so that those gentlemen who are now giving what they consider shorter hours than the rest of the tradesmen should have no reason to complain. (Hear, hear.) With regard to competition he would say that all experience of labour movements showed that the reduction of the ,hours of labour in a reasonable way, and as the tinges demanded, did not lead to lessened production. (Hear, hear.) With the nine hours movement generally adopted, they had a greater production throughout.the world than was ever known in the world's history before. Were they to be told that what had been done with the manual classes of labour could not be done in their case? He ventured to say that what held good with the working-classes generally, held good equally as well with shop assis- tants. (Hear, hear.) He was astonished to hear that 90 per cent, of the tradesmen of Warrington were in favour of the movement. He should not call that a beginning ;it seemed like a magnificent ending. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Already as large a proportion were read/ to adopt that movement in War- ringtnn as they had in Chester. (Hear, hear.) In 1890, 396 towns in the United King- dom had adopted and were carrying out the half- holiday movement, but to-day 528 towns had adopted it. If thev continued that work in the spirit they had begun it, before three months were over that 528 would be made into 529. (Loud applause.) The. re.nlation was then put to the meeting and car- ried unanimously ard enthusiastically. Councillor 11. ROBERTS moved, That this meeting respectfully solicits those proprietors who are willing to close their sh pa one half-day per week to do so on Thursday the 24th day of this month at one o'clock in the afternoon, irrespecsive of the few who refuse to do so, and hereby requests the public to do their purchasing for the future before one o'clock on Thursdays.". (Ap- ple flee.) Haying referred to the great advantages of a half- holiday, he remarked that when once the thing lsad be- come eqatlished he ventured to say that the receipts of the sh.pkeepers of Warrington would not be less than they 'here to-day, but might be somewhat greater.

(Hear, bear.) With regard to the letter of Aid. Francomb he must say that he did not like the idea of the shop assistants of Warrington having to request as an occasional privilege that which the hours of their em- ployment, which expediency, and which experience, proved to be not simply a necessity but an absolute right. (Applause.) Because some shopkeepers in Warring- ton would not close their shops was no argument against the half-holiday. As there were blacklegs in every work- shop, so there were blacklegs in every trade. (Hear, I hear.) There were shopkeepers in Warrington—he was glad to say they were very few—who would grind the very last penny out of their customers and the very last effort out of their assistants. (Hear, hear.) He added that, though they might not publish a list of the shop- keepers who would not close their shops, they could, at all events, publish a :list of those who did, leaving the public to find who were left out. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) .

Councillor Saw Gummi, in seconding the proposal, said that one great reason why the markets were not closed earlier on a Saturd.ly night was that public-houses were so late in closing. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Rev. J. GUNNELL supported the resolution, and referred to the benefits which had resulted in some of the towns in which he had lived from the half-holiday movement.
Mr. S. KHNYON also supported the resolution, and alluded to the long hours which he had himself worked when an assistant.
The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried with acclamation.
A vote of thanks to th• Chairman, moved by Council- lor Roberts, and seconded by Mr. Stanley, brought a succeastul and enthusiastic meeting to a close.

div.head: COAL TRADE CRISIS.
div.p: COAL TRADE CRISIS.
BEGINNING OF' THE STRUGGLE.

The first step in the struggle between masters and men in the Durham coal trade was taken on Wed- nesday, when one of the collieries in the west part of the county was stopped. The men struck because the owners issued a notice that no more coals would be given to workmen, who at all collieries are sup- plied free. Throughout the county of Durham the result of the balloting, so far, is in favour generally of a strike. Lord Londonderry's and Lord Durham's men have declared for a strike in overwhelming numbers. Several colliery villages in the county are supplied with water for all purposes from the pits. If a stoppage takes place, and the colliery enginemen are withdrawn, as intended, there will be both a coal and water tamine.

The position of affairs in London is unchanged. No rise was made in the price of fuel on the Coal Exchange on Wednesday, hut, owing to the very severe weather prevailing, hawkers increased the price by id. per cwt. Block fuel has increased 75 per cent. The price of wood has also risen.

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKS.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKS.

Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., have made the follow- ing announcement in their works :—"ln consequence of the stoppage of work by the colliers, we have received notice that all our supplies of fuel will cease on and after Saturday, March 12th. It will be necessary to let the mills and forges stand except such portions as we are able to provide suitable fuel for ; and we therefore give notice to the workmen that our engagements will terminate on Saturday next, 12th March." The result of this notice will be that from this afternoon, most of the men employed by the firm will be suspended from work, a few furnaces only being kept going. Should the coal strike continue another week, there may be a complete stoppage. So far as Messrs. Pearson, Knowles, and Co. are concerned, the engineering works at their Hallam and Bewsey forges will be continued in opera- tion as usual, their works including the fitting shop, foundry, and wheel and axle departments, but with re- gard to the forge departments themselves, results will depend upon the action of the men employed by the firm at their collieries. To-day will,however,decide matters. The Whitecrws works, the company owning which have collieries of their own, will go on as usual. Messrs. Wands Brothers works and the Cockhedge mills are not as yet affected.

div.head: WIONES, &c.
div.p: WIONES, &c.

The strike of colliers is likely; to have a disastrous effect upon the Chemical trade of Widnes and Runcorn. If the strike continues the whole of the work will be stopped and at the present time a number of the de- partments in several of the large works have been stopped and there are some hundreds of men out of work. Those who wish for coal for domestic use have to pay is. 3d. per cwt.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, St. Helens, states that all the colliery proprietors in the district have con- sented to allow their men to work from Tuesday and Wednesday, which are the make up days and the days upon which the fourteen days' notice given expires, until Saturday. It is probable that the men will work on Saturday, and then cease work for whatever period the conference to be held on Wednesday week determines, though it is generally felt by those able to form an opinion, that this period will not be longer than a week. In the St. Helens district stocks have been worked down, and there is every hope that after the stoppage work will be brisk for the miners. An impression appeared to prevail among some people that the local miners were averse to coming out, but Mr. Glover stated that this was not so. On Saturday morning, Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Limited, proprietors of collieries at Haydock, Ashton, Golborne, Edge Green, and Havannah (Parr), gave notice to their agents in Liverpool, Birkenhead, Manchester, Warrington, and other places that they intended to in- crease the price of all qualities of coal by half-a-crown a ton. In connection with the closing of the old glass-werks at Ravenhead and Sutton, on Wednesday, the 1,500 hands who were stopped were not told when work would be resumed, neither were they told what amount, of re- duction was contemplated when they came back. The St. fßflens colliers are working on daily contracts until Saturday afternoon, their fourteen days notice having expired on Wednesday.

div.head: THEATRE ROYAL, WARRINGTON.
div.p: THEATRE ROYAL, WARRINGTON.
RE-OPENING UNDER NEW MANAGENI.ENT.

On Wednesday evening the Theatre Royal, Scotland- road, which has been leased for four years from the proprietress, Mrs. Sheridan, by Mr. J. W. &ape, pro- prietor of the Britannia Theatre, Garstoq, was opened under his new management, after undergoing consider- able improvement. The building has been undergoing a course of repainting and re-decorating, Mr. W. Hoult, of King-st., carrying out this work. It has been re- upholstered by Mr. T. Cavanagh, of Manchester, and new scenery, executed by Mr. Snape himself, has been provided. The theatre now presents a much more cheer- ful and lightsome appearance, and the improved appoint- ments have much enhanced the comfort of the building The performance on Wednesday night was announced to be under the patronage of the Mayor (Alderman E. Greenall), but the lessee was informed that his wor- ship would be prevented from being present through having been called away to London. At the entrance to the threatre, over the door, appeared, in the form of gls illumination, in celebration of the occasion, the letters J.W.S., the initials of the lessee. There was a large attendance, and the principal piece was the drama of Drury Lane celebrity "The Jewess, or the Council of Constance," a work which is replete with passages and incidents of thrilling and absorbing in- terest. The scene is laid in Italy, the pniod represented being some centuries back. The plot turns upon the circumstance of Prince Leopold (Mr. J. H. Barrett), a Christian, the son of the reigning emperor, becoming enamoured of Rachael, the Jewess (Miss Lottie Blackwell), and courting her incognito, and en- deavouring to induce her to fly with him. She ultima- tely consents, but he afterwards changes his mind, and finally informs her that this is because he loves another, and leaves her, she recumbent on the ground, having fainted at the news. There sl,e is found by the Princess Eudosia, the neice of the emperor (Miss Amy Copeland) who takes her to the imperial palace as one of her servitors. Here she discovers her lover in the person of Prince Leopold as he is on the point of being married to the Princess. She denounces him in the pre- sence of Cardinal de Brognie (Mr. G. Taylor), as haying, he being a Christian,committed,by making the advances he had done for alliance with a Jewess, a breach of the Gentile ecclesiastical law,, the penalty for which is death Her supposed father, Eleaza (Mr. G. Cooper), admits haying countenanced the offence and all three are sen- tenced to death by torture. Rachel, however, her old love reviving, and stung by remorse, accuses herself in order to save his life, of having calumniated him, and her father supports her in the retractation, the result being that the prince is acquitted, and the Jewess and her father only stand condemned by the Cardinal to death. At the last moment the Jew saves Rachael and himself by identifying her to the Cardinal as his own daughter, who he supposed had perished when an infant in a fire in his palace at Rome. The part of the Jewess was well-sustained; and that of the Jew especially so; that of. the Cardinal also was sup- • ported in dignified and becoming style. Mr. Barrett evoked much applause in his part of the Prince, and Miss Copeland made a very good Princess. Mr. Snaps as John Forester, a merry and easy-going Englishman, always ready' as he expressed himself, to "uphold the honour and glory of old England," happily relieved the somewhat sombre nature of the piece, with his frequent characteristic sallies, and seemed a favourite with the audience.—The drama was succeeded by a most laugh- able farceentitled "Captain's not a-miss," which went exceedingly well, and was a decided hit. We may men- tion that a good band was in attendance under the leadership of Mr. Frank Ellerton. "Under Two Flags" and,'" Hanle Kirke" are an- nounced for the ensuing week. Particulars' will be found in our advertising columns.

div.head: 131 Tom o' Mac 0' BOB'S.
div.p: 131 Tom o' Mac 0' BOB'S.

The Yankees lick creation ! They're nod content wi' supplyin' us wi)" Mag- nets" as prove varra attractive, but neaw they're ackshally bringin' eawt a nyin machine ; an' a scor- cher its beawn to be. Aw'm thinkin' o' advertisin' my railway shares (L. an' Y.) nod becoseo' th' divvy bein' low, or on ackeawnt o' th' condition o' th, rowlin' stock, but becose every train, tram, an' booat 'ill be eawt o' date afoore so varra long; there'll be nooan to be sin onywheere, except i' Museums.

--Just think heaw grand id'ill be when we con o' on us fly, like th' butterflees an' birds do,—an' hens an' wasps. There's bin odd times when aw've flown eawt o' th' heawse when th' wife's bed her monkey up, an aw wonst med a chap fly seven or eight yerds ; he'd come to beg a subscription to'rt Booth's querter ov a million peawnd. Aw supplied th' propeller, an' he went off like a shot in deawnward direction ; some fooak wod argy as he were nobbut obeyin' th' laws o' gravitation, but aw tell yo' he flew—an' i sich a way as no amateur fotograffer gcoin' could ha' ten a "instantaneous "on him. Id'ill be nice when th' childer con fly after but- terflees, i'stead o' hevin' to chase 'em wi' their jackets as we used to do in owden times ; they'll miss o' th' disadvantages o' th' owd style—sich as bangin' ageean lamp-pooasts, an' missin' catchin' the butteaflee, after o'. • _ .

There's nobbut one thing as puzzles this Yankee inventor, an' it's so little it's herdly wo'th mention- in', but it's th' state o'th air as bothers him aboon a bit; id seems as id owt to be one atom—or a tooa- " gigantic atoms "—for good sustainin' peawer, but th' Yankee discovered as it's bin put together wi' miserable looseness. That's a little matter fr Yankee to remedy; he wor'nd pre- sent to glum* is vallyable suggestions at th' time o' th' creation, but he con step in neaw wi' his im- provements. Yo'll find Professor Langley's idea i• th' "North American Review," (an' rare an' silly stuff id is) an' aw see as the Manchester Literary an' Felosofickle Society's bin discussin' th' subject this week. Well, it's a gret pity they he v'nd sum- mat better to do.

There's varra little as is new i'th pappers this week, so far. There is some unequal sentences re- poorted i'th' Liverpool peppers —some as'll nod werk eawt reight by simple proportion, but that's nowt new.
_ Then there's a Inshurance Company bin try n' to wriggle eawt o' nayin a claim, but that's nowt new. _

An there's no end o' suicides, an' child morthers, and some o' them's new, especially them as is traced to lowness o' epirits browt on by Inflooenza. geddin' serious when yo' cum to think o'th num- ber o' ca. E. there's bin, an' heaw Horrible they are; doctors seem to be useless, becose i' one case id were a doctor hissel' as committed suicide.
_ Id proves as fooak as is recoverin' fro' Tnflooenza want keerful nossin%—an' watchin' clooasely. * * *

An' aw see as th' toy revolver noosance is still goin'. Three lads were browt up at Salfoid last Toosda'—two on 'em 16, an' t' other 14 year owd— cherged wi' firm n one P th' streets th' fleet afoore ; they were let off becose their patents promised to give 'ern a good leatherin'. Th' magistrate said ditto to wod aw said a tooathri week sin'; he said "he was sorry there was no Act of Parliament under which he could deal with the prisoners, and he thought the law ought to be so altered as to restrict the indiscriminate sale of these dangerous weapons to mere children and boys. If magistrates had the power to inflict a smart tine—say of £so—upon dealers who sold revolvers and firearms to persons under 20 years of age, it would be of very great service to the community." Every sensible mon an' woman 'll say " ditto."

Just a word or two on theayter gooin'. There's a lot o' fooak—an' varra sensible fooak, too, i' some things—as thinks as gooin' to th' theay- ter is th' same as gooin' to th' Owd Lad ; an' there's I a lot o' varra sensible fooak as thinks just collywest, Yo' see, th' theayter is nobbut a buildin' med o' I same stuff as yo'r own heawse, or a cherch, but these fooak as thinks play gooin' sich a bad thing argy as it's th' bad fooak yo' meet wi' theere ; well, they met just as weel ax yo' nod to walk through th' street for th' same reason. Then, they say, yo' see an' hear things as isn'd fit to be heeard an' sin, an' childer heal. an' see 'em as wed l ; well, this is them soort o' fooak's own fan't, becose iv nob'dy went to hear an' see sich rubbisn there'd be varra little on 't written. A lot o' these objectors wod sing hymns to th' tune o' "John Breawn's body lies a-mow- derin' i• th' grave," but they wodn'd join i' th' chorus o' sich a lively comic song as "Auld Lang Sync." They oiez mek me think o' Macaulay's descri2tion ov a Puritan (stown, aw think, fro' Hume) as bein' a chap as objected to bull-baitin', nod on ackeawnt th. pain as id gi' to th' hull, but on ackeawnt o' the pleasure as id gi' to th' spectator. Eawr stage plays sprung fro' th' owd miracle plays as were fest, played moore nor 700 year sin'; an they're nod o' on 'em eawt o' date yet, for th' Passion Play at Ober-Ammergau draws bigger creawds every time as it's played. Ov coourse there's bin evolution at werk as far as plays goon, an' it's mony a time hap- pened as the waikest hes gooan to th' wo'; but for o' thad he's i' poor health as corn'd see a moral pointed an' a tale adorned in a good play. Avv reckon sich a play as !` Drink " to be a lot better nor a scoore o' teetotal lectures, becose th' audience geds interested i' th' werkin' mon as tawlts teeto- talism to his shopmates. an' that's wod they dorn'd olez do wi' a weel-dressed lecturer. Aw reckon to be a owd codger wi' some religion carcase, but aw mon confess as Shakespeare con gi' me moore pleasure nor mooast o' paysons as aw happen to know; an' as for fun—well, a young chap'll find "The Gav'tior " heattier nor kliss-F-th'-ring, an " Dorothy " better nor sich childish tackle as "Shy widow" and "French tig."
THE PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COM- PANY, LIM[TED.

A summary of the reports presented at the forty- third annual meeting of this great compam , will be found in our advertising columns. Details are there given which evidence the progressive char• acter of the business of the company. The number of policies issued during the year was 58,118, assuring the sum of £5,932.493, and producing a new annual premium income of £355,980. The premiums received during the year were £1,442,746, being an increase of £280,097 over the year 1890. The increase in the premium raceipts for the quinquennium 1887-91 was £1,045,806. giving an average annual increase of £209,161. The claims of the year amounted to £387,106. The number of deaths was 2,734. In the industrial branch the premiums received during the year were £3,688,338, being an increase of £170.413. The increase in the premium receipts for the quinquennium 1887-91 was £777,043, giving an average annual increase of £155,408. The claims ot the year amounted to £1,647,300. The number of deaths was 183,927. The total number' of policies in force was 9.817,484, the average duration being six years and three-quarters. The total assets of the Company are £14,823,627, being an increase of £2,043,757 over those of 1890. The directors point out that during the five years under review the assets of the Company have grown from £6,811,954 to £14,623,627, showing an enormous increase of £7,811,673. The annual premium income of both branches combined, at the beginning of the quenquennium,was £3,472,911, and at the end £5,386,990, being an increase of £1,9/4,079. It will be conceded that the above figures fully uphold 'the reputation of the Company as the most gigantic of its kind in the world. We have only to add that Mr. J. Lythgoe, of 69 Sankey-st„ is thetenergetic and courteous local superintendent.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

At this Court on Thursday, before his Honour, Judge Ffoulltes, Messrs. Millington and Owen, exe- cutors of the late Wm. Owen, a farmer who resided at flaydock. brought an action against John Owen, farmer, for the sum of £2O ss. 6d. being the balance of amount due from the defendant as incoming tenant of Canal Farm, Haydock, lately occupied by the de- ceased. The plaintiffs alsc> claimed delivery of a silver watch and chain, a double-harrelled gun and a set of swingle-trees, which were valu.d at £5 es., which were alleged to be the property of the testator and detained from the executors by the defendant. The defendant counter-claimed for the sum of £49 7s. 2d. in respect of wages due to him, funeral expeases, Ser. Mr. Unsworth of the firm of Me.srs. Jenkins and Unsworth, repre- sented the plaintiffs, and Mr. Hatton (Messrs. R. Davies, and Co > defended. After a prolonged hearing a verdict was given for the amount claimed £2O 5.. 6d., and for delivery up of the silver watch and chaiu, or its value £3 ; and on the counter-clai:n the defendant was awarded £l2Bs. Lord Denbigh pagsed away peacefully at Monks Kirby, Warwickshire, on Thur3day morning.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

THE CRAIG DIVORCE SUIT. The divorce suit of Craig v. Craig and Ramp was concluded in London yesterday, when the Judge gave a decree nisi with costs, and the husband was awarded £5O damages against the co-respondent. CHARGE AGAINST A SOLDIER.

At Manchester, yesterday, Edward Holden, an sx- quarter-master sergeant in the Royal Engineers, was charged on remand with having incited a soldier to dis- close information respecting the defences of Malta. The prisoner was again remanded.
KIRBALDY ELECTION. The following is the result of the polling, yesterday : Dalziel (Liberal) Cox (Unionist)

Liberal majority... 1036 SENTENCE ON MR. HASTINGS, M.P. At the Central Criminal Court, on Friday, Mr. George Woodyatt Hastings, M.P. (66), was indicted for con- verting to his own use upwards of £21,000, of which he was trustee. Mr. Justice Smith said no doubt prisoner had been plundering the trust of the late Major Brawn for years, bringing to the verge of want those who be- lieved him to be a man of honour. He, therefore, sen- tenced him to five years' penal servitude.

THE BLACKMAILING BY AN OXFORD TUTOR. At the Central Criminal Court, London, yesterday morning, before Mr. Justice Smith, Maitland Francis Moreland (65), of 23, John-st., Oxford, pleaded guilty to attempting to obtain money from Earl Russell by menaces, but not guilty to the indictment charging him with attempting to obtain £7O from Lord Hothfield by false pretences. The court was crowded. Mr. Gill briefly sketched the case for the prosecution, showing that it was prisoner's plan to try and draw his victims into correspondence under the name of Mrs. Moreland, and afterwards to demand blackmail for the return of the letters. Mr. Justice Smith said he was aware of the prisoner's age, but was unable to pass a less sentence inan ten year's penal servitude.
TERRIBLE PIT EXPLOSION IN BELGIUM. FEARED ENORMOUS LOSS OF LIFE. 300 MEN ENTOMBED.

MONS, FRIDAY.—A terrible explosion of fire-damp oc- curred this morning in No. 3 pit of the Anderlues Col- liery, in the province of Hainanit. BRUSSELS, FRIDAY, 2.3o.—The latest news from Ander- lues gives it that there were 300 men in the pit at the time of the explosion. The disaster is believed to be much greater than at first stated. The volunteers have been unable to penetrate into the workings. Three women who worked in the pit as colliers have been brought out alive, but it is feared that all the others in the colliery have perished. Intense excitement prevails in the district, and thousands of workers from the ad- joining pits are flocking to the scene.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met soon after four. The Marriage abroad Bill, and Roads and Bridges (Scotland) Bill were read a second time. The House adjourned at five minutes to five.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS,
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS,

The Speaker took the chair at two o'clock. BIRMINGHAM WATER SUPPLY.—On the motion of Mr. T. Ews, it was agreed to commit the Birmingham Corporation Water Bill to a Select Committee of nine members empowered to take evidence for and against the bill. EMPLOYERS LIABILITY BILL.—The Home Secretary, answering Mr. Aird, said he hoped to introduce the Em- ployers' Liability Bill at no distant date. The Local Authorities Acquisition of Land Bill was read a third time, and the sitting was suspened. ARMY ESTIMATES —Considerable discussion took place as to the suggested increase of the pay of private sol- diers, and the condition of the army generally which was taken part in by Sir W. Harcourt„ Mr. Buchanan, Mr. Campbell Bannerman, Col. Nolan, Mr. Stanhop3, and others. ANOTHER GOVERNMENT DEFEAT. The House wont into Committee of Supply. Mr. McNeill brought up once more the question of the votes of Sir L. Pelly, Sir J. Puleston, and Mr. Burdett Coutts in the division on the Mombass Railway vote last week and moved that their votes be disallowed. After some remarks from Mr. Balfour, Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Goschen and Mr. Norton, the House divided.
For the motion Against ................... ........
Majority for the motion 5 - The result was received with loud Opposition cheers. The votes were then disallowed.

div.head: BUCKLEY-STREET CHAPEL, WAR RINGTON..
div.p: BUCKLEY-STREET CHAPEL, WAR RINGTON..

Saturday was a red letter day at this place ; A tea meeting was held and waa attended by about 150 persons. The following ladies pre- sided at the trays :—Mesdames Simpson, Prow, Fairhurst, Adams, Scott, Urniston, Drury, Wood- ward, and Hall. After tea a unique entertainment was given by the Rev. James:, Hall, of Liver- pool, entitled "A Manx Musical Story," (of which he Is the author) assisted by the ehoir,whose capttal rendering of the various pieces elicited very hearty applause. Mr. A. Leech presided at the harmonium and Mr. H. Trow at the piano. Mr. J. E. Trowaran sang" The beautiful city," and Mr. Hall " The grave- digger," and," Rock'd in the cradle of the deep," and were loudly cheered. The chair was taken at 730, by Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S., who was supported by Mr. John Griffiths, as deputy chairman. The Chairman's remarks were warmly received and highly appreciated. He *as glad he said to be able to do them service in trying to remove the clebt,and was very pleased to know from Mr. C. Simpson, the secretary of the chapel, that they were 'tatting on so well with their subscriptions and donations since they began to attack the debt. He alluded to the cost of being religious and the cost of not being religious. It was often said that it was. a costly thing to attend reli- gious services, but that, he contended, was not the case when all the Sides of the question were looked at,, and reckoned up properly. Jost let them reason that out for a minute or two. For the sake of his argument. he should presume that all in that room were worshippers in one place of worship.oill another, and that all of them contributed in accordance with their means and gene- rosity. coopers, or silver,, or gold in support of the place they attended, and the minister who conducted the ser- vice. Dare anyone tell him that an equal nuchber of ,people„with the same income and with like responsibi- lities 4itt home, who,, instead of attending a place of .worship, or meeting, like that one, went tdithe Music Mail or the taproom and drank more than was; good for them, were as well off as they were? Decidedly not! They were not so clean' not so well behaved; not so well dressed ;not so regular in, their habits, or attentive to their duties;" It Was those virtues that went to make the steady, sober-minded. working-man. (Applause.) There was always more pre& in being godly than there , was in being ungodly. tHear; hear, and applause.)— Mr. John Griffiths then took Mr. Morris's plaee as Chair- man, as he had an engagement at another place.—Mr. GRIFFITHS+ said he was pleased to see such a good gather- ing, and to be with them et such an enjoyable as well as profitable entertainment. He engaged to do whar, lay in his power te help them in their laud- able work. Mr. Hall' then gave a story entitled " God's Christmas box.' Mr. Simpson in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Hall and the choir, &c., and which was supported by Mr. TJrrnston and the vice-Chairman, gave a verbal report of the state of progress which had been made sineo Mr. Hall gave them his lecture on Dec. 13th.. They had secured a reduction of one per cent, on the old mortgage. Their Chairman, Mr. Morris, was giving £lO and he (Mr. Simpson) received on Saturday,. a cheque from Mr. W. D. Houghton for £5, and a pro. rnise from Mr. F. Monks of £lO as soon as they had raised £ll5, and he (Mr. Simpson) assured them that they were going to fetch that £lO. Already with the pro- ceeds of their tea they had raised £BO towards the debt. (Loud cheers.) And they hoped by May to announce at their annual tea that they had secured Mr. Monk% 10, and were in more satisfactory circumstances than they had over been before. - -

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. CitotY Orrice : HOLBORN BARS, LONDON. SUMMARY of the REPORTS presented at the FORTY- THIRD ANNUAL MEETING held on 3rd March, 1892. ORDINARY BRANCH.—The number of Policies issued during the year was 58,118, assuring the sum of £5,932,40, and producing a New Annual Premium Income of £355,980. The Premiums received during the year were £1,442,746, being an increase of £280,097 over the year 1890. The in- crease In the Premium receipts for the Quinquennium 1887-91 was £1,045,806, giving an average annual increase of 2209,161. The Claims of the yeas amounted to £387,106. The number of Deaths was 2,784. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH—The Premiums received during the year were £3,688.338, being an increase of £170,413. The increase in the Premium receipts for the Quinquennium 1887-91 was £777,043, giving an average annual increase of £155,408 The Claims of the year amounted to £1,647,300. The num- ber of Deaths was 183,927. The total number of Policies in force was 9,617,484 the average duration is six years and three quarters. The total Assets of the Company, as shown in the Balance Sheet, are £14,623,627, being an increase of £2,043,757 over those of 1890. The Directors have agsin prepared a supplement to the Report, showing in detail how the assets of the Company are invested. The Balance Sheet has again been submitted to th. inde- pendent professional audit of Messrs. Deloitte, Dever, Griffiths, 8c Co., whose certificate is appended to the Accounts. SUMMARY OF THE QUINQUENNIAL REPORT. FOR THE PERIOD ENDING 31sT DECEMBER 1891. The Directors have much pleasure in submitting their Re- port, and that of the Actuaries of the Company, upon the valuation of the Company's assets and Liabtlities, which has just been completed. As on previous occasions, the processes and results of the valuation have been submitted to Mr. A. H. Bailey, and his report is also attached. During the Five years now under review the Assets of the Company have grown from £6,811,954 to £14,623,627, being an increase of £7,811,673. The annual premium income of both Branches combined, at the beginning of the Quinquennium was £3,472,911, and at the end £5,386,990, being an increase of £1,914,079. The valuation of the Ordinary Branch has been made upon the same principles as those of the preceding Quinquennium; namely, a net premium valuation on the Institute of Actuaries' (H.M.) Table of Mortality for the life risks, and Mr. Finlaison's Government Annuity Table, 1884, for the annuities, the rate of interest in both cases being 3 per cent. The valuation of the Industrial Branch has also been made on the basis of a net premium valuation at 3 per cent, interest, the Table of Morality being Dr. Farr's "English Life Table," No. 3. At the beginning of the Quinauennium a revision of the Tables of Assurance was made considerably in favour of those of the assured who keep their policies in force for five years. These increased benefits have been made retrospective, and. as will ho seen from the Actuaries' Reports, a corresponding Increase has been made iu the necessary reserves. --- Extract from Mr A. H. BAILEY'S Report. The time having arrived at which another valuation is required to be made of the liabilities of your Company. I inspected, during the progress of this immense work, the various processes that had to be adopted for the purpose, and the results have been submitted to me for examination. On the 31st December, 1891, the total number of assurances in force was 9,880,103, besides 1,557 grants of annuities. By the last Census it was ascertained that the total number of persons living on the sth April, 1891, in the United Kingdom was 37,740,283 ; so that, after making allowances for the cases in which two or more Policies have been granted upon the same life, it appears that the lives of about one-fourth of the population of Great Britain and Ireland are assured by your Company. The numbers have increased by more than 37 per cent during the Quinquennium now under review. The nods that have been accumulated to meet these liabi- lities amount to £14,087,303, exclusive of the Proprietors' capital. The principles upon which the liabilities have been esti- mated are those now generally adopted by well-conducted Assurance Companies. The basis of valuati n has my full concurrence, and having been set out in the Actuaries Re- ports, together with the results in the case of each Branch, need not here be repeated. Extract from the Reports of Messrs. T. C. Dewey, W. HUGHES. and F. SCILOOLINo, the Actuaries of the Company. ORDINARY BRANCH.—The number of Life Policies in force at December 31st. 1891, was 262,619, assuring, with bonus, £28.570,567, and producing a gross annual premium income of £1,487,344. The results of the Valuation are as follows : Life Assurance Fund on the nit December, 1891 ...£5,505,095 Reserve for Llfe Assurance Policies, including reserve for immediate pats ment of claims... £3,983.469 Reserve for Annuities ... „, 502,241

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF TEE DARESBURY DIVISION LADIES AND GESITLEMEN,—I wish to tender my sincere thanks for the honour you have done me in again returning me to the County Council as your representative. I assure you I appreciate highly the confidence evidenced by my un- opposed return. I shall endeavour to justify that confidence by using my best efforts in the interests of this division, and by working to promote the welfare and prosperity of us all. I have the honour to remain Your faithful servant, WILLIAM R. BARI% Preston Brook, sth March, 1892.

CHESTER COUNTY 'COUNCIL ELECTION TO THE ELECTORS OF RUNCORN NORTH DIVISION. LADIES AND GENI Lamism, —I beg to tender my heartfelt thanks to the large number of electors who so nobly sup- ported me by their votes on Saturday last. Although my supporters did not quite achieve the success they so well deserved, they fully demonstrated that on a future occasion when I again hope to solicit their suffrages they will secure a triumphant victory. My special gratitude is due to many friends who worked so zealously and unsel- fishly on my behalf; but they will probably find their best reward in the remarkable proof their exertions gave of the great vitality and strength of the Liberal party under some- what untoward conditions in the North Division of Runcorn. Faithfully yours. W. OCKLESTON. Halton-road. Runcorn, March 13, 1892.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE RUNCORN NORTH POLLING DISTRICT. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I beg to thank you most sincerely for the great honour you have conferred upon me in placing me at the head of the Poll on Saturday last, thereby renewing your confidence in me. I assure you it is my firm determination to faithfully represent the whole electorate, and trust that by so doing I shall convince you all that your confidence was not misplaced. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours Faithfully, CHARLES W. HAZLEHURST.

LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF NEVVION-IN-MAKERFIELD DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLIMEL—You have conferred upon me the honour of electing me your representative in the County Council. For this mark of your confidence, I beg to tender my sincere thanks and I hope my efforts to carry out the trust you have reposed in me will always meet with your approbation. Gentlemen,—l have now had your Marsh's Patent Smoke- consuming Stove for 18 months in constant use, and the longer we use it the better we like it, and for cleanliness and comfort it is a great contrast to the open fire. I aysp rather sceptical in regard to its not requiring the chimney sweep- ing. but having watched it very carefully for over 12 months. I am now sati fled that it does all that your advertisement says it will do, for I have not had the chimney swept since it was put in, and it keers its draught ; and so I find that not only does it save fuel, but the dirt, cost, and inconvenience of the sweep.—Yours truly, JOHN A. THISTLETHWAITE. -- 322, Leeds Road, Bradford, January 15, 1892. Gentlemen,-1 have two of your Marsh's Patent Smoke consuming and Fuel-economising Fires at work continuously in my establishment. One fire has been fixed for fourteeg months, working two large ovens (one heavy cast iron and one sheet iron), and the other is applied to a complete bakers range, with large ovens, side boiler, and hot plate, and they have both given every satisfaction. After getting the fires well started with nuts, we use practically nothing but smudge on the two-decker, and nuts and smudge on the range, for the remainder of the day. The heat obtained from this inferior coal with this Patent fire is really marvellous ; indee,i, one can hmlly realise tfie fact of being able to bake bread and pastry with common smudge. Previous to having these Fires we had to sweep the chimney every two months, but it is now fourteen months since we had it swept, and so far as I can judge, there will never be any necessity to sweep it again.—Yours truly, TRELFA. COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 AND 1886. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Monday, the 7th day of March, 1892,— IT WAS ORDERED, pursuant to the power contained in Article 11 of the Foot and Mouth Disease Order of 1892, and with the view of preventing the introductien of Foot and Mouth Disease into the district of this Local Authority, that the movement by land or by water of Cattle,Sheep,Goats,or Swine into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester from the Counties or Places hereinafter mentioned shall, from and after the Seventh day of March, 1892, BE ABSOLUTELY PROHIBITED until this order is revoked, that is to say— City of London County of London County of Middlesex County of Surrey County of Sussex County of Southampton County of Kent County of York (West Riding) County of Edinburgh County of Lanark The Island of Sheppey Or out of any county, or place where Foot and Mouth Disease exists, or has existed within 14 days from the date hereof, or shall hereafter appear, and also from the District of any separate Local Authority, situate wholly or partly within any of the before-mentioned Counties or Places. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 7th March, 1892. The foregoing Regulations do not restrict the move- ment of Animals by Railway through the District of the Local Authority of this County without untrucking. Any offence against the above Regulations is deemed an offence against the Act of 1887, which renders the offender liable to a penalty of not exceeding Twenty Pounds.
